en: The Bodhisattva’s Samādhi of Mindfulness of the Buddha Sūtra, Scroll One.
Translated by the Song Dynasty Indian Tripiṭaka Master Guṇabhadra.
Chapter One: The Introduction. Chapter One: The Introduction.
Thus have I heard:

At one time the Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha on Vulture Peak Mountain, together with a great assembly of one thousand two hundred and fifty bhikṣus. All were arhats—whose outflows were exhausted, who were free from further afflictions, self-controlled and at ease, well-liberated where there is nothing more to be liberated from, possessing profound knowledge of what is not to be known, having accomplished what was to be done, having attained the state of no-self, having laid down their heavy burdens, having destroyed the nine fetters, being definitively liberated, and having mastery over all minds like great dragons—with the sole exception of Ānanda.

At that time, the devaputras Nanda, Sunanda, Candana, Sumana, Īśvara, Maheśvara, Ajita, and Caryā—along with countless other devaputras from the Śuddhāvāsa heavens—their radiance at the end of the night was twice their usual brilliance, and Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa suddenly became brilliantly illuminated.

Then the sons of the gods went to where the World-Honored One was; with single-minded reverence, they prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and scattered over him various celestial fragrances—fine powdered sandalwood, *tāmālapatra* and aloeswood incense, celestial flower garlands, and various floral scents such as *kustuma*.
He bowed his head again at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him three times to the right, withdrew to stand to one side, and joined his palms toward the Buddha.
At that time, the Devaputra Candana silently formed this thought:
“All Buddhas of the past have expounded for the devas, worldlings, śramaṇas, and brāhmaṇas the Bodhisattva’s Recollection of the Buddha Samādhi as taught by all Buddhas.”
He further thought:

"Now our World-Honored One, like all the Buddhas of the past, should also proclaim the Bodhisattva’s Samādhi of Mindfulness of the Buddha for the sake of bringing peace and happiness to the people and devas of the world."
Then all the devaputras addressed the Buddha together, saying:
“World-Honored One!

All Buddhas of the past have taught the Bodhisattva’s Samādhi of Mindfulness of the Buddha, which brings peace and happiness to the world and its eight classes of beings, including gods and humans. We only pray that the World-Honored One, like the Buddhas of old, will extensively expound this samādhi for the sake of sentient beings.”
At that time, the World-Honored One granted his consent by remaining silent.
Then the sons of the gods circumambulated the Buddha three times, prostrated at his feet, and suddenly vanished.
At that time, when the night had passed and the signs of dawn appeared, the World-Honored One smiled with a serene countenance and let out a great lion’s roar.

By the Buddha’s spiritual power, the monks residing separately on Vulture Peak all arrived at the Buddha’s location; the bhikṣuṇīs of the great city of Rājagṛha, moved by the Buddha’s majestic voice, also assembled together. King Ajātaśatru of Magadha, along with the son of Brahmā, Śreṇika, and surrounded by immeasurable billions of followers, likewise, by the Buddha’s spiritual power, arrived at the Buddha’s location in a single thought-moment.

Furthermore, there were the yakṣa kings Āravaka, Ghaṭapa, Kiṃpila, Śūlipāla, and Māratāli; such yakṣa kings possessed great supernatural power, each with hundreds of thousands of retinues. By means of the Buddha’s spiritual power, they arrived at Vulture Peak Mountain in a single moment of thought.
Furthermore, there were the asura kings Rāhu, Vemacitra, Śumbha, and Prahāraka, along with their retinues.

In this manner, throughout the trichiliocosm, the gods, nāgas, and nāga kings—immeasurable and boundless—were struck with wonder; their hair stood on end in solemn awe, and by the Buddha’s spiritual power, they arrived at the Buddha’s dwelling in a single thought-moment.

In the eastern world-systems, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, the Brahmā devas and celestial kings, hearing the Buddha’s coughing and clearing of his throat, were struck with solemn awe such that their hair stood on end; they went to where the Buddha was.
It was likewise so in the remaining three directions, as well as in the zenith and nadir.
At that time, the elder Anāthapiṇḍada Sudatta also went from Śrāvastī to where the Buddha was, accompanied by countless hundreds of thousands of attendants.
At that time, there were great elders in Vaiśālī named Subhadra, followed by Arindama, and then Śrī;
there were also Licchavi princes named Haribhadra and Gajapati.
Furthermore, there was a śūdra official named Prabhākara;
all such as these were students of the Mahāyāna, and together with immeasurable multitudes, they went to the place where the Buddha was by virtue of the Buddha’s spiritual power.
At that time, in the city of Campā, there were sons of commoners named Śikṣā and Upakāra;
there was also a son of a great householder named Anantabala.

These and others among the assembly had already planted various roots of goodness in the past and possessed great majestic power; sustained by the Buddha’s spiritual authority, they went to where the Buddha was.

At that time, immeasurable sentient beings in Vārāṇasī, whose roots of merit planted in former lives had now reached maturity, proceeded from Vārāṇasī in continuous succession, walking on foot to the place where the Buddha was. They prostrated themselves in salutation and stood in attendance at his left and right.

At that time, in the great city of Kuśinagara, there were immeasurable Mallas and sons of Mallas who, having already made offerings to various Buddhas in the past and planted roots of various wholesome karmas, possessed great majesty and virtue. Proceeding from Kuśinagara in harmonious accord, they followed the path in succession until they arrived at the place where the Buddha was; with sincere hearts and deep reverence, they came forward and prostrated themselves at his feet.
At that time, through the Buddha’s supernatural power, the three-thousandfold great thousandfold world system became perfectly equal in length and breadth.

All eight classes of beings—gods, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharva kings, asura kings, garuḍa kings, kiṃnara kings, mahoragas, and so forth—all gathered there in assembly, leaving no empty space between them.

At that time, the World-Honored One, seeing that the assembly had gathered, again let forth the great lion’s roar and emerged from the monastery to approach another place; seeing from afar that the ground in that direction was composed of various jewels, the World-Honored One smiled once more.

Immediately, the people of the world, the devas, and the asuras each took immeasurable powdered incense and various flowers and scattered them over the Buddha, paying homage with utmost sincerity, reverence, and praise.

At that time, the assembly was fully gathered, including the Elder Śāriputra, the Elder Mahāmaudgalyāyana, the Elder Mahākāśyapa, the Elder Subhūti, the Elder Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra, the Elder Rāhula, the Elder Mahākaṅkara, the Elder Mahākātyāyana, the Elder Aniruddha, the Elder Kapphiṇa, the Elder Luṇo Viṃśatikoṭiputra, the Elder Nanda, and the Elder Ānanda—all of whom possessed majestic virtue and were endowed with supernormal powers. Such a multitude of noble ones had all assembled together.

At that time, among the assembly were the Elder Maitreya Bodhisattva, Trailokya Bodhisattva, Trailokyasamatikrānta Bodhisattva, Sadyahprathamacittotpādacakrapravartin Bodhisattva, Sucintita Bodhisattva, Mahāghoṣasvara Bodhisattva, Dharaṇīdhara Bodhisattva, Mañjuśrī-kumārabhūta Bodhisattva, Amoghadarśin Bodhisattva, and others such as these, numbering in the infinite and boundless. They had all made offerings to past Buddhas, deeply planted countless bodhisattva practices and vows, and long since resolved their minds upon supreme enlightenment.

At that time, the Elder Bodhisattva Amoghadarśin, wishing to understand the signs of the Tathāgata’s supernormal power and the meaning of his smile, adjusted his robes, circumambulated the Buddha three times, withdrew to stand to one side, and with palms joined toward the Buddha,
spoke these verses: "O Most Victorious One, Unconditioned, World-Honored One among bipeds, For the sake of those to be tamed, You manifest this gracious smile."
The wealthy can bestow kindness and cause the poor to be satisfied; when the Buddha expounds the gift of Dharma, his radiance likewise shines forth.
He is the one to whom all worlds turn for refuge; by what causes and conditions does he manifest this smile?
"Unsurpassed Perfect Enlightenment—may you explain this for me.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Akṣayamati:
"Do you see that ground of various jewels over there?"
Amoghadarśin replied,
“Indeed, I have seen it. “So it is, Amoghadarśin!”
"That land is precisely where the Buddhas of the past traveled and transformed beings.
At that time, Akṣayamati thought to himself:
"I should proceed with all haste to that place."
In accordance with that manifestation, his mind entered samādhi.
Having entered samādhi, he conjured for the Buddha, the World-Honored One, various Dharma-thrones made of many jewels.
Having established the thrones just as he had intended, he went to where the Buddha was and entreated the Tathāgata to ascend this jeweled throne, saying:
“World-Honored One!
This place is the ground where all the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, of the past, present, and future have trod.”

At that time, the World-Honored One went to that place and took his seat upon the Dharma-throne. In a single thought-moment, by the power of the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, this trichiliocosm shook in six ways—it surged, surged everywhere, and surged equally everywhere; it quaked, quaked everywhere, and quaked equally everywhere; it roared, roared everywhere, and roared equally everywhere; it trembled, trembled everywhere, and trembled equally everywhere; it swayed, swayed everywhere, and swayed equally everywhere; it rose, rose everywhere, and rose equally everywhere—surging in the east and sinking in the west, surging in the west and sinking in the east, surging in the south and sinking in the north, surging in the north and sinking in the south, surging in the west and sinking in the east, surging in the east and sinking in the west, surging in the north and sinking in the south, and surging in the south and sinking in the north. A brilliant light shone universally throughout immeasurable worlds.
In a single thought-moment, all sentient beings, even those in the Avīci Hell, experience complete happiness.
As the Buddha ascends the Dharma seat, he shines like the radiant sun;
he is the one toward whom all the worlds turn in devotion. The great trichiliocosm trembles, and all give rise to joy.
The Buddha ascends the precious throne, Radiant like the sun;
All the worlds revere the Dharma King, Desiring that all sentient beings Universally obtain peace and happiness.
Once the Buddha had taken his seat, he was as radiant and clear as the sun;
honored by all the worlds as the Dharma King, he emitted pure light that illuminated all buddha-fields.
How marvelous!
This vehicle is the most supreme among all vehicles;
how extraordinary!
This vehicle is unsurpassed;
wherever it briefly appears, its extent is already immeasurable.
How excellent!
This vehicle—vast and great—is the vehicle by which one rides.
Those who ride this vehicle are inconceivable; even the devas, Māras, and Brahmās cannot fathom them.
At that time, the World-Honored One extended his broad and long tongue, which completely covered the trichiliocosm, and addressed the śrāvakas and the assembly of bodhisattvas:
“O sons of good family!
Listen with single-minded attention.

That night, the devaputras Nanda, Sunanda, Candana, Sumana, Īśvara, Maheśvara, Ajita, and Carita—along with countless other devaputras from the Śuddhāvāsa heavens—appeared after the latter part of the night with a radiance twice their usual splendor, causing Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa to suddenly blaze with light.

At that time, the devas came to where the Buddha was; with single-minded reverence, they prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and scattered over him various celestial fragrances—fine powdered sandalwood, *tamālapatra* and aloeswood incense, celestial flower garlands, and various floral scents such as *kūṣmāṇḍa*.

He bowed his head at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him three times to the right, and then stood to one side with palms joined toward the Buddha, making offerings, showing reverence, honoring, and praising him.
At that time, the Devaputra Candana silently gave rise to this thought:

"The Buddhas of the past—the Arhats, the Samyaksaṃbuddhas—all expounded for the sake of humans, devas, śramaṇas, and brāhmaṇas the Bodhisattva’s *Buddhānusmṛti-samādhi* (Samādhi of Mindfulness of the Buddha) as taught by all Buddhas. Now, our World-Honored One should likewise follow the example of those past Buddhas to bring peace and happiness to sentient beings by proclaiming the Bodhisattva’s *Buddhānusmṛti-samādhi*."
When the sons of the gods had thus made this request, I granted my consent by remaining silent.
In this manner, monks, the son of the gods Candana, the son of the gods Nanda, and the various sons of the gods from the immeasurable Pure Abodes, knowing that I had consented, suddenly vanished.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"He addressed the bhikṣus:
'The radiance is twice its usual measure; Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa has suddenly become brilliantly illuminated.'"
They made offerings, showed respect, and surrounded the Lord of the World.
There were the devaputras Sunanda, Sumati, Candana, Īśvara, Maheśvara, and Ajita.
The Devaputra Sukṛtakārin and others such as these, immeasurable in number—
Śuddhāvāsakāyika devaputras possessing great supernormal powers— have come to my presence.

With rare and wondrous offerings, they all paid their respects together; circumambulating him three times to the right, they prostrated themselves with their heads at his feet and withdrew to stand to one side.
Having remained silent for a while, he resolved to act for the sake of teaching and transforming sentient beings,
and requested that the Bodhisattva’s *nien-fo samādhi* (Buddhānusmṛti-samādhi) be expounded:
"For this has already been taught by the Buddhas of the past."
Excellent!
Śākyamuni, Tathāgata of the Ten Powers, you have taught this samādhi so that all beings may attain peace and happiness.
The Buddha granted his consent by remaining silent; at that time, the sons of the gods already knew that he had graciously agreed.
I, too, here on Vulture Peak, shall [expound] the samādhi as it was taught by the Buddhas of the past.
He silently consented; filled with joy and happiness, he circumambulated him three times to the right, prostrated at his feet, and departed.
Do not give rise to doubt or uncertainty regarding the wisdom of the Tathāgata, which is like that of all Buddhas of the past.
Inconceivable are the past Buddhas; regarding supreme enlightenment and all knowledge and vision, their minds are free from the net of doubt.
Now, in the present, regarding this foremost enlightenment, I have fully understood it, and my mind is free from obstruction. As for future ages,
should one wish to achieve enlightenment and desire to act out of compassion for the sake of future generations,
I likewise understand this clearly, and my mind is without even a hair’s breadth of doubt.
Therefore, the Tathāgata possesses an inexhaustible and profound understanding; his power of wisdom is unimpeded and inconceivable.
Of that which he knows, I have fully exhausted all details, yet all sentient beings cannot fathom its depths.

**Chapter Two: The Past Deeds of Amoghadarśin** At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Elder Śāriputra, the Elder Maudgalyāyana, the Elder Mahākāśyapa, the Elder Subhūti, and the Elder Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra:
“The devas and the people of the world have all already assembled. You bhikṣus, each ascend the Dharma-seat and let out the lion’s roar.”
"Why is this? Because all these many śrāvakas, upon hearing the lion’s roar, have attained liberation.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Maitreya Bodhisattva, Vyatīta-trailokya Bodhisattva, Acintya Bodhisattva, and Amoghadarśin Bodhisattva:
“You should now request the Tathāgata to proclaim the lion’s roar of the true merits taught by all Buddhas.
Akṣayamati said, “So be it, World-Honored One!”
"Indeed, I have heard it.
He then spoke this verse in praise:
"The color of his body is like gold, Adorned with a hundred merits; Out of compassion for us,"
Having fully realized the ultimate truth, you are endowed with all virtues and your fame flows afar.
World-Honored One, for what cause and condition do you cause me to pose this question before this great assembly today?
The Perfectly Awakened One is peerless; there is none superior to Him, the Dharma-King of merit.
His great wisdom is inexhaustible; He has tamed the world.
For what reason, amidst this great assembly, do you cause me to inquire?
The Tathāgata’s pure precepts, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation are all entirely peerless.
Now our Sugata, for what cause and condition, within this great assembly, has prompted me to inquire?
O World-Honored One, Dharma King, who has attained the further shore and is able to bring great benefit to sentient beings.
"Sugata! For what reason do you cause me to pose this question before the great assembly?
Having cultivated loving-kindness for a hundred kalpas and familiarized myself with the sphere of compassion, my eloquence is unimpeded."
Sugata! For what reason have you caused me to pose this question before the great assembly?
That the poor may obtain wealth, the blind may regain their sight, and that the agony of suffering may cease forever.
Fearing [suffering] and seeking peace, by what causes and conditions am I moved to ask this question?
The Buddha’s body is pure and wondrous; it is untainted by dust or defilement.
The Tathāgata’s robe is of various mixed colors;
the World-Honored One’s lineage is the king among kings.
By what causes and conditions should I be prompted to inquire?
The robes worn by the Buddha remain four finger-widths away from his body, yet they do not leave it; his body is able to subdue all enmity.
By what causes and conditions does this come to be? May I ask you this question.
In the sphere of the Tathāgata’s activity, there are no pits or ravines; by the power of wisdom, all that he treads upon is level.
By what causes and conditions have I been prompted to inquire?
The body of the Tathāgata neither increases nor decreases;
his gait is level and upright, neither crooked nor bent.
It transcends all ordinary beings and is inconceivable.
For what reason do you prompt me to inquire?
Gazing up at your venerable countenance, my eyes do not for a moment wander.
Your movements require no effort; by the power of your spiritual feet, your majestic deportment is spontaneous.
The schools and academies may be admired.
Yet, if one is seized and held by *piśāca* demons or *kumbhāṇḍa* spirits, one becomes bewildered and loses one's mind, remaining without any awareness or discernment;
but if one beholds the World-Honored One, in a single thought-moment, all evils are forever abandoned, and one regains right mindfulness.
If there are sentient beings who touch the dust of the Buddha’s feet, for seven months their bodies and minds will experience bliss;
after the end of their lives, they shall be reborn in a favorable realm. Taking refuge in the World-Honored One, he bestows all happiness.
If there is someone who is ill and suffers extreme agony, the Buddha touches them with his hand and they are immediately healed.
Over vast eons, the Sugata has fully attained all inconceivable and innumerable peace and happiness.
The Buddha was once valiant; he gathered together the pure dharmas attained throughout immeasurable kalpas of the future.
Regarding this matter, I have no doubt or hesitation.
By what causes and conditions have I been prompted to inquire?
Among the gods, you are preeminent; now, having encountered the Tamer, the Great Seer among men.
"By what causes and conditions have you prompted me to ask this question?
At that time, the World-Honored One told Akṣayamati:
"Listen attentively, listen attentively, and reflect upon it well."
Amoghadarśin replied,
“So be it, World-Honored One!
The Buddha then addressed Amoghadarśin:
"I recall that in the past, incalculable kalpas ago, there was a king named Anantabala (Limitless Power), who possessed great supernormal powers and sovereign authority.
This king established a great city as his residence; the city was named Supratiṣṭhita (Well-Established) and measured twelve yojanas in both length and breadth."
The city has seven tiers, each side having three gates; these gates and the city walls are all adorned and magnificently decorated with gold, silver, lapis lazuli, crystal, agate, pearls, and coral.
The moats are also sevenfold, all made of the seven treasures.
Outside these gates, the ground is strewn and adorned with gold and silver sand; on both sides of each gate, there are four golden and silver towers facing one another.
"In this way, Aśūnya-darśin!

Furthermore, great nets made of gold and silver were spread over the gates; the golden nets hung everywhere with silver bells, and the silver nets dangled here and there with golden bells. When the wind blew through the bells and nets, they all produced sounds like those of the kōng-hóu lute and other musical instruments, with the *gong* and *shang* notes flowing harmoniously and in perfect accord."
Once the king had completed the city, he settled within it.
Outside the moat of this city were seven ponds, composed of gold, silver, crystal, and coral.
These various ponds have seven tiers of paths, which are likewise adorned with the seven precious substances:
the golden paths have railings of silver;
the silver paths have railings of gold.
The stairways were made of silver with railings of pearls;
the stairways were made of pearls with railings of lapis lazuli;
the stairways were made of crystal with railings of coral.
The stairways were of coral with railings of pearls;
the stairways were of pearls with railings of gold.
Thus it was, O Aśūnya-paśyin!
King Anantabala planted various extraordinary flowers:
utpala, padma, kumuda, puṇḍarīka, and nalinī flowers; their fragrance was harmonious and gentle, and there was no one who begrudged them, so they could be gathered at will.

On the banks of that pond were various kinds of flowering trees, namely: *icchantika* flower trees, *nicula* flower trees, *kadambinī* flower trees, *atimuktaka* flower trees, *campaka* flower trees, *pāriyātraka* flower trees, *kovidāra* flower trees, and *dhānuṣkāri* flower trees.
The fragrance of these flower trees is like celestial incense, and they are without guardians;
one may take them as one pleases. Furthermore, Ānanda-vimaladarśana!
This city of Sugṛhīta has sevenfold rows of tala trees, all interspersed with the seven precious gems.
The *kadamba* trees have silver leaves, flowers, and fruits;
the silver *kadamba* trees have red pearls for leaves, with their flowers and fruits being likewise;
the white pearl trees have lapis lazuli for leaves, with their flowers and fruits being likewise.
The lapis lazuli trees have crystal leaves, and their flowers and fruits are likewise;
the crystal trees have agate leaves, and their flowers and fruits are likewise;
the agate trees have red pearl leaves, and their flowers and fruits are likewise.
The red pearl trees have coral for their leaves, and the same is true for their flowers and fruits;
the coral trees have gold for their leaves, and the same is true for their flowers and fruits.
"Aśūnyatādarśin!
When the wind blows through the trees, they strike against one another and produce a subtle and wondrous sound, just as a skilled musician is able to strike forth the five kinds of musical tones."
"Furthermore, Aśvaghoṣa!
In the place where the king dwells, these various sounds are constantly uninterrupted:

the sounds of elephants, horses, chariots, and armies; the sounds of conch shells, drums, flutes, and pipes; and the sounds of lutes, biwā, singing, and dancing—such diverse sounds have never ceased for even a moment."
The king constantly issued a proclamation to the people within his realm:
"If there is anything you require—whether clothing, food and drink, or elephants, horses, and carriages—grant it all to you according to your wishes."
"Between the tala trees, the sounds of music constantly emerge; the people roam there, delighting themselves with the five desires.
The king regards his subjects as a father thinks of his children, and all serve the king as if he were a compassionate father."
"Furthermore, Aśvaghoṣa!
Within the city of Supratiṣṭhita, streets, lanes, villages, and marketplaces were laid out.

At every location there were also ponds made of the four jewels, each separated from the next by the distance of a single arrow-shot. The four banks of these ponds featured stairways made of various precious gems."
The golden steps had silver railings, and the silver steps had golden railings; likewise, they were interspersed with crystal and coral.
Furthermore, Anagata-darśin!
The king planted various famous flowers in all the ponds, and further planted diverse flowering trees upon the banks of those ponds.

There were *ini-ja* flower trees, *kadambara* flower trees, *atimuktaka* flower trees, *campaka* flower trees, and *dhānu-kārī* flower trees; their fragrance was like celestial incense, yet no one cherished them as their own.
Within the city, various gardens and groves were also constructed, with diverse flowers and fruits arranged in rows among them.
Furthermore, throughout the four directions of these gardens, there were exquisite flower ponds everywhere, likewise adorned with the seven treasures as described before.
There were many court ladies who entertained one another, and all the people enjoyed themselves as they pleased. Furthermore, Anagha!
King Aparimita was a noble scion of a great Kṣatriya lineage; from his parents down through seven generations of ancestral descent, his lineage was entirely pure.
His countenance was upright and elegant, preeminent among men; his wealth and treasures numbered in the billions, beyond all calculation.
"Furthermore, Anagata-darśin!

King Aparimita-bala possessed profound faith and vast benevolence; with an open mind, he practiced great giving, bestowing upon śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, as well as upon the blind, the deaf, the mute, the crippled, those afflicted by a hundred ailments, the poor, the orphaned, and those in distress."

The eighty-four thousand cities and villages over which the king ruled were adorned with the seven treasures as the fruit of his pure karma; atop each city, he further constructed eighty-four thousand exquisite watchtowers made of sandalwood.
Outside these gates, four-way roads were opened, and at the head of each road, magnificent and beautiful towers and pavilions were erected, where all the people could sport and play as they pleased.

Day and night, lamps and candles were lit throughout the multi-storied pavilions, towers, palaces, streets, lanes, villages, and hamlets; their brilliant and intense light illuminated the entire realm, and the sentient beings who received this radiance experienced joy in both body and mind.
"Furthermore, Aśvaghoṣa!
The king had two sons:
the first was named Siṃha, and the second was named Siṃhamati. They had long ago made the vow for unsurpassed bodhi; their fame was heard afar, and they were endowed with great majesty and virtue."

At that time, there was a Buddha named Ratnaskandha Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidhyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān, who appeared in the world and proclaimed:
"In this world and in future worlds, among the great assemblies of śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, devas, humans, and asuras, I possess all-knowing vision."

He universally preached the wondrous Dharma for all living beings—a teaching that is good in the beginning, middle, and end; excellent in its phrasing and meaning; and fully endowed with the characteristics of the pure and holy Brahma-conduct—accompanied by seven hundred *koṭis* of great arhats, all of whom possessed supernatural powers and sovereign majestic virtue.
"At dawn, the Tathāgata Ratnaskandha adjusted his robes, took up his alms bowl, and entered the city to beg for food, accompanied by a retinue of bhikṣus."
At that time, King Anantabala, together with his two sons, was enjoying himself in pleasure upon a high tower.
From afar, the king beheld the Buddha’s marks and signs of merit; a sense of wonder arose within him, and he rejoiced beyond measure.
Surrounded by their retinue, they went together to the palace gate and told their two sons:
"Quickly take fragrant flowers, banners, streamers, and musical instruments, and hasten to where the Buddha is."

He then immediately offered gośīrṣa sandalwood, powdered incense, and various wonderful and rare treasures to the Buddha and the community of bhikṣus; he circumambulated them three times to the right, prostrated with his head at their feet, and withdrew to stand to one side.
"Furthermore, Aśvaghoṣa!
The king and his two sons invited the Tathāgata Ratna-skandha and his assembly of śrāvakas, providing them with all necessities for their comfort for as long as they lived.
After the Tathāgata Ratna-skandha had completed his teaching among devas and humans, he was about to enter parinirvāṇa."

At that time, knowing that the Buddha would not remain long in the world, the king, accompanied by his two sons, ministers, subjects, and retinue leading and following him, arrived at the place of parinirvāṇa. When the Tathāgata had already entered extinction, he prostrated himself with his head at the feet in reverent salutation, wailing and weeping piteously, throwing his body upon the ground like a collapsing great mountain, and cried out:
"The Eye of the World has been extinguished!"
Again, he lamented with deep sorrow:
"The eye of the world has been extinguished!
How swift is the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa!"
"It is as if a merchant has lost his master; so it is when the Buddha passes into extinction.
The world is plunged into darkness, blind and devoid of the eye of wisdom.
Beating his breast and striking his head, he raised his voice in a great cry, sobbing and wiping away his tears as he addressed his two sons:
"Prepare various fragrant baths to wash the Tathāgata.

Furthermore, they anointed his body with various exquisite perfumes; they scattered all manner of flowers and floral garlands, and wrapped the Tathāgata’s body in immeasurable, wondrous robes. They prepared a coffin made of the seven precious gems and an outer casket of iron; they gathered red sandalwood to a height of one yojana, with a length and breadth each exactly one krośa.
Furthermore, he scattered flowers and incense over the pyre and poured a thousand vessels of ghee over the sandalwood; only then did he kindle the fire.
Once the flames had burst forth, he wailed and lamented once more, shedding tears like rain.
At that time, Siṃha thought to himself:
"The World-Honored One has entered parinirvāṇa; what would my life be for?
I, too, shall follow the Buddha and enter parinirvāṇa."

Having made this vow, he once again scattered various rare and wonderful incense and flowers over the pyre. Wrapping his body in white cotton cloth and holding a torch in his hand, he threw himself into the fire. As the flames blazed fiercely, for the sake of benefiting sentient beings and taking refuge in the World-Honored One, he spoke these verses as a prayer and praise for the Tathāgata:
“Like a great mass of precious jewels, The one honored by the world, With the suffering of birth and death forever ended, He has entered parinirvāṇa herein.”
From this day forward, we shall no longer behold the turning of the Wheel of Dharma.
The Dharma King whom I served has already entered Nirvana;
the proclamation of the vast and profound meaning can never again be disseminated.
When shall I, amidst the great assembly, hear the teaching of Bodhi?
May the devas and the people of the world rejoice and praise these well-spoken words;
from this day forward, may the sound of inconceivable [worldly] discourse cease for me.
The Supreme Tamer of the World has sunk into extinction here;
Nāgas, devas, asuras, and kinnaras,
Who once rejoiced and constantly sang his praises, Shall no longer hear this sound.
The poor have attained fulfillment, and those in suffering have received protection;
now that the World-Honored One enters nirvana, we have all lost our refuge.
Our father, King Unmeasurable Power, and his younger brother Siṃhamati—
There is likewise no longer the shade of his compassion, nor do I hear him preaching the Dharma anymore.
I too shall follow the World-Honored One and swiftly attain parinirvāṇa;
since the path of the world is shrouded in ignorance, what use is there in this painful birth?
Now, by burning this poisonous body, I vow to attain the inconceivable.

In the past, together with my father the king, I constantly made diligent offerings to the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha throughout the long night; now I have obtained the fruit of that retribution.
If I have cultivated various virtuous deeds in the presence of the Buddha,
it is for the sake of taming the world and attaining the inconceivable.
To cause all sentient beings to give rise to inconceivable vows:
When the World-Honored One enters parinirvāṇa and I cast myself into the blazing flames,
whoever sees or hears of this shall all attain Buddhahood—
except for those who slander with malice and those who have already realized the stage of right certainty.
If I cultivate the vast and immeasurable practices of a bodhisattva,
may all sentient beings who see me even in a dream attain the path of Buddhahood—
except for those who slander with wrong views and those who have already realized the stage of certainty.
This body is like a mass of foam; death is certain for all.
Should any among the countless classes of sentient beings eat my flesh, they shall all swiftly attain Buddhahood.
While I was practicing the bodhisattva path,
those who reviled me with harsh words encountered a Tamer of Men; they shall certainly attain Buddhahood,
except for those who slandered with malice or those who had already realized the stage of certainty.
If a person, regarding my body, cultivates the contemplation of loving-kindness and compassion and seeks the supreme enlightenment,
they shall swiftly attain the path of Buddhahood—
except for those who slander with malice and those who have already realized the stage of non-retrogression.
By means of these conditions for burning my body, seeking the fulfillment of both my own and others' vows,
if my mind is truly sincere, may I immediately see the Buddha arise again.
Should I behold the Buddha once more, may he remain in the world just as he did before.
When I cast my body into the fire, it was just as when I previously attended the Buddha.
The Buddha arose in his true form; what I see now is no different from before.
Only then did I realize that the Buddhas are continuous and never severed.
I only pray that the Honored One with the Universal Eye, out of compassion, will gather in and protect this world.
Knowing the prince’s heart and his most earnest and profound longing,
the Buddha immediately exerted his great supernormal powers from within the mass of flames.
As he arose from samādhi, his radiance became doubly brilliant;
the inconceivable multitude all marveled at this unprecedented occurrence.
For the sake of those gathered there, he further brought about great benefit.
Having completed the work of transforming those to be converted, he returned to enter nirvana.
Having seen the Buddha display his great majestic spiritual power, the Lion was filled with profound joy;
his body and mind were serene, blissful, and at peace.
Deeply knowing the teachings of all Buddhas, which are inconceivable, the Tathāgata,
though having entered nirvāṇa, still accords with the wishes of sentient beings.
"Inconceivable are his precepts, concentration, wisdom, and liberation."
As well as the knowledge and vision of liberation, his spiritual transformations are immeasurable.
Taking refuge in the World-Honored One, one should thereafter cast off the body.
His sublime deportment in the world is most excellent and without peer.
With sovereign spiritual powers, you are likewise without equal;
when the Tathāgata entered parinirvāṇa, all were struck with alarm and lamentation.
Therefore, with a sincere heart, I take refuge in the Honored One of Universal Vision.
I take refuge in the Sugata, the Lord who has exhausted all defilements;
I take refuge in him who is forever free from suffering and who compassionately regards the world.
With perfect wisdom he observes all things, thoroughly understanding and knowing the minds of others.
He eliminates the diseases of all afflictions and brings accomplishment to immeasurable multitudes.
The Great Physician, Honored Among Men, bestows inconceivable medicine;
he is able to skillfully remove all the ailments and sufferings of the world.
I take refuge in the unsurpassed Teacher, who has compassion for all sentient beings.
If I were to praise the Tathāgata’s merit in even a single thought-moment,
or the virtue of burning my body as a tiny hair, or the blessing of making an offering for but a brief instant—
"May all such pure deeds as these be bestowed upon all beings. "In this way, Aśvaghoṣa!

At that time, the devas, Māras, Brahmās, and all other people of the world saw the Lion cast himself into the blazing fire; they were all struck with great sorrow and alarm, and gave rise to a sense of wonder."
After his life ended, he was immediately reborn in the Brahma Heaven, possessing great supernormal power, majesty, and sovereignty.
At that time, this Brahma thought to himself:
"How is it that I have suddenly been reborn here?"
He reflected once more:
"In the past, among human beings, I already served the Tathāgata Ratitāskandha, honoring, respecting, revering, and praising him with a sincere heart."
After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, he cremated his body as an offering, further reciting verses and making great vows; by virtue of these wholesome karmas, he was reborn in the Brahma Heaven.
I shall now go to the place where he cremated his body.

At that moment, the Brahmā suddenly vanished; in the time it takes a strong man to flex or extend his arm, he arrived at the site where the Tathāgata had been cremated. He took celestial sandalwood, aloeswood, powdered incense, kusuma flowers, and tamālapatra, along with countless varieties of fragrant flowers, scattering them everywhere through the air like falling rain. They swirled in all ten directions like wind-blown snow as he made offerings to the relics of the Tathāgata Ratnaskandha.
He spoke of his past causes and conditions to the King of Infinite Power:
"I am the body of Prince Siṃha—who cast myself into the fire as an offering and passed away—only I pray that Your Majesty does not regard me with compassion."

I have now obtained all manner of wholesome benefits; by virtue of the fruit and reward of my past merit—having served, honored, revered, and praised the Tathāgata Ratitāśa with sincere devotion—I have been born in the Brahma Heaven.

Therefore, Great King, you and Siṃhamati should together treasure, respect, uphold, and maintain the sublime Dharma; collect the relics and distribute them for veneration, ensuring that none are left behind and that no indolence arises.
"Great King, you should know that when I was born in the Brahma Heaven, I also constantly revered, upheld, and received this supreme Dharma.
Having spoken these words, he suddenly vanished.
Furthermore, O Akṣayamati!

King Anantabala and Siṃhamati took water to extinguish the fire, and made various offerings with exquisite incenses, myriad flowers, precious garlands, banners and streamers, and musical performances.

In a mere instant, eighty-four thousand cities and towns were completely filled with eighty-four thousand stūpas and temples, all exquisitely adorned and embellished with the seven precious treasures.

These jeweled stupas were one yojana in height and exactly one krośa in length and breadth; around each and every stupa, eighty-four thousand lamps filled with various fragrant oils were lit, and between these stupas, offerings of various kinds of incense, flowers, and music were made as before.

Out of respect for upholding such a sublime Dharma, King Anantabala, by virtue of these roots of goodness, did not fall into the evil realms throughout eighty-four thousand kalpas alongside Siṃhamati. Furthermore, during eighty-four thousand billion kalpas, he drew near to and made offerings to sixty thousand buddhas, honoring them in succession without interruption, and in every lifetime he constantly became a wheel-turning sage king.
"Furthermore, Aśvaghoṣa!
After the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata Ratna-skandha, there appeared in the world a bodhisattva named Samantaguhya-rāja."

Out of compassion for the world, he left the household life to study the Way; beneath the Bodhi tree, he sat cross-legged with a single-minded concentration, attaining liberation through right wisdom and awakening fully to the unsurpassed path.
"Furthermore, Aśvaghoṣa!

This Brahmā Siṃha went to the presence of the World-Honored One, the Buddha Samantaguhya-rāja. Abiding in the air, he made offerings to the Buddha with celestial sandalwood, circumambulated him three times to the right, prostrated himself in salutation, and requested him to turn the Wheel of Dharma, saying to the Buddha:
'I only pray that the World-Honored One will arise from the site of enlightenment, subdue all the armies of Māra, and remain unhindered in his pure spiritual wisdom.'"
May the Teacher of the World, out of compassion, awaken from meditative absorption and, as a Tamer, instruct the assembly of liberated śrāvakas by expounding the exquisite Dharma of the Sugata.
Having long cultivated wisdom and embraced wholesome dharmas in previous lives, the Tathāgata has now become the Honored One among men.
In past lives, you already made this great vow:
"When I attain Buddhahood, may I deliver those who have not yet been delivered.

Now that your vow is fulfilled, you have attained the state of peace, the most supreme unconditioned, and tranquil, wondrous bliss; you shall now open the gate of the Deathless to untie the three fetters of the multitude.
At that time, the World-Honored One silently granted his consent.
Then, that Great Brahmā and the countless devas, knowing that the Tathāgata was about to turn the wheel of Dharma, were all filled with joy and leaped for immeasurable delight.
At that time, Brahmā prepared various sublime offerings and immediately made a great vow seeking the unsurpassed path:

"May I encounter the Samantaguptarāja, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha; may he give birth to a mass of pure and wondrous merit within me, and by this karmic fruit, may I always be able to draw near to and behold the Buddhas of the ten directions throughout the cycle of birth and death."

If I make offerings to the Bodhi tree of the Buddha, may you, out of compassion for me, preach the Dharma for me regarding these various merits I have cultivated; by the fruit of this retribution, may I always be able to praise the stupas and temples of the Buddhas throughout the cycle of birth and death.
"Furthermore, Aśvaghoṣa! Prince Siṃha burned this body of his;

by virtue of these merits and the roots of goodness he cultivated, he dwelt eternally in the Brahma-world, where he encountered five thousand buddhas, making offerings to them, serving them with reverence, honoring them, and praising them. He planted various roots of goodness and made inconceivable vows."
“Āśūnya-darśin, do not give rise to such doubt. Who else could that King Anantabala have been at that time?
It was none other than my own self.
Then Āśūnya-darśin addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Are these two princes still present now,
or have they already attained parinirvāṇa?
“Indeed they have, World-Honored One!”
"I pray that you will explain this for me. He told Akṣayamati:
"The prince Siṃhamati at that time was none other than Maitreya."
The one who was Siṃha at that time was you yourself.

Having cast off this body, Prince Siṃha, within the Dharma of the Tathāgata Ratna-skandha, taught and brought to maturity thirty thousand sentient beings, establishing them in the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"Recalling a past life, there appeared in the world The one named Ratnaskandha-Amitalocana, Who brought vast benefit to all beings."
Adorned with a hundred merits and golden in hue, out of compassion and pity,
having deeply understood the true reality, he reveals the profound Dharma for the sake of delivering all the world and rescuing sentient beings from suffering and affliction.
The Jewel-Shouldered One, the Perfectly Enlightened One, the Honored One of all worlds,
and the assembly of Sugatas of the three wheels— seventy-two billion in number—
together with this great multitude, entered the city and shared in the protection.
In the past, there was a great king named Anantabala (Limitless Power),
who possessed sovereign majesty and authority, and whose might could subdue all.
The king, together with his two sons, went out to wander upon a high tower and pavilion.
From atop his palace pavilion, the king gazed afar at the Tamed Sage,
the Jewel-shouldered Teacher of Gods and Men, attended by his assembly of bhikṣus.
Then the king, together with his two sons, quickly went out to welcome the Honored One among Men.
Having arrived at the place where the Tathāgata was, he immediately prepared an extensive and wondrous offering.
He prostrated himself, circumambulated him three times, and then stood back with palms joined.
He invited the Buddha and the assembly of monks to accept his service for as long as he lived.
With garments and delicacies, the most rare and precious things in the world,
for eighty-four thousand years, they offered these without ceasing.
At that time, the king and his two sons calmed their minds and sought Bodhi.
When the Buddha had passed into parinirvāṇa, they collected his venerable relics and,
for the sake of that Buddha Ratitāśva, reverently constructed stupas made of the seven precious gems.
There were eighty-four thousand of them, exquisite, most elegant, and sublime.
At each and every stūpa, he lit eighty-four thousand lamps.
Then King Anantavīrya, at the site of the Sugata,
offered incense, flowers, and various musical performances with a profound heart of devotion.
Having already planted inconceivable and immeasurable roots of goodness,
and having served sixty thousand Buddhas— the refuges of all worlds—
he sought with utmost sincerity the foremost, unsurpassed, and supreme enlightenment.
"O Bhikṣu!
Do not harbor doubt. In the past there was a king; you, who are so wise and discerning, should not give rise to a different view.
He of that time with immeasurable power is none other than my own self."
With various flowers and manifold incenses, and by lighting lamps bright day and night,
for the benefit of Jambudvīpa, they made offerings to all the Tathāgatas.
Their giving was never insufficient, and their hearing of the Dharma was likewise so.
Never having harbored thoughts of indolence, you sought bodhi with single-minded devotion.
The Honored One of Perfect Enlightenment, the Jewel Shoulder, possesses unsurpassed, great, and clear wisdom.
In the past, you once burned your own body as an offering to the Great Sage.
Casting oneself into the midst of fierce flames, one initially feels no pain or fear;
burning the body like a wick, with oil dripping upon it,
it is consumed gradually rather than all at once, just like the wick of a pure lamp.
For the sake of benefiting sentient beings, you made offerings to the Buddha of Nirvāṇa.
That Buddha had already cremated his body; you knew the skillful means to entreat him, and beholding the Buddha arise from the fire, his radiance became even more manifest.
Seeing the Buddha no different from before, a mind of reliance and trust arose;
immediately casting off this body for the benefit of all, he thought:
"If I shall indeed fulfill this vow, I shall revere the Buddha just as I did before."
The various merits thus obtained are inconceivable.
If I possess past vows and have gathered the karmic fruits of previous lives in their hundreds,
thousands, and tens of millions, I shall surely behold the Buddha.
If my vow is true, the Buddha should arise from the fire.
The Buddha’s wisdom is exceedingly pure; ultimately free from defilement and attachment, it is serenely and eternally extinguished, its continuity never interrupted.
Knowing that the Lion’s mind was pure, the Buddha first illuminated his intention;
then the Buddha rose from the fire, his marks and signs even more extraordinary.
O Bodhisattva Amoghadarśin!
Once the Protector of the World had arisen, all aspirations were fulfilled without exception.
He further made a vow; that vow was inconceivable, beyond the reach of calculation or enumeration.
Out of compassion for the world, the Lord of Dharma arose from amidst the fierce flames;
by the inconceivable power of the Sugata, his radiance was even more sublime.
At that time, the entire assembly was filled with utter astonishment.
With a purified mind, he uttered a great exclamation, leaping for joy in a way never before experienced:
"How marvelous!
Your great supernormal powers are peerless in their might; the realm of the Buddha is profoundly deep and inconceivable."
When one thousand sentient beings, having witnessed this miraculous manifestation,
no longer grasped at any phenomena and attained excellent liberation of mind— O Aśūnyadarśin,
you should know that the Lion [has acted] for the sake of the world.
When the Buddha was requested to rise again, one thousand sentient beings,
in the presence of that Sugata, beheld the Buddha’s miraculous transformations;
their minds were correctly directed toward the path of unsurpassed bodhi.
Having extensively performed benefits for the world through great compassion,
the Buddha returned to nirvana.
The lion also relinquished its body, and at the moment of death, was suddenly reborn in the Brahma Heaven.
The Brahmā descended from above, scattering celestial sandalwood powder as an offering at the site where the Tathāgata was cremated.
After the Jewel-Shouldered One had passed into parinirvāṇa, there appeared a Buddha named Samantaguhya-rāja.
The most supreme among the honored ones of humanity, the Great Seer among the celestial kings,
has appeared in the world out of compassion for sentient beings.
This Buddha, having sat beneath the Bodhi tree and attained perfect awakening, [remains there].
Brahmā prepared exquisite delicacies and made offerings to the World-Honored One;
bowing his head to touch the Buddha’s feet in prostration, he entreated the Buddha to turn the wheel of Dharma.
The Tathāgata King of Universal Mystery immediately understood the mind of Brahmā.
He granted his consent in silence.
The Brahmā was filled with great joy and, at the place where [the Bodhisattva] burned his body, made further great vows.
This Brahmā had already cultivated inconceivable merit.
In the past, during the course of one kalpa, he made offerings to five thousand Buddhas;
with a sincere heart he revered the World-Honored One and attended upon the Honored One among Men.
He further addressed Akṣayamati:
If you possess wisdom, do not give rise to divergent views:
he who was Brahmā in the past is none other than your own self today.
Of the five thousand Buddhas of the past who have entered parinirvāṇa as Sugatas, [you are one].
I see you all clearly: before each and every Buddha, you have burned your bodies as an offering, seeking supreme enlightenment.
Of the many thousands of Buddhas of the past who entered parinirvāṇa and left behind their relics, [you have honored them all].
In the presence of such Buddhas, I sacrificed my body, hands, and feet.
For the sake of benefiting sentient beings, I cultivated the bodhisattva practices;
whether in recent times or in distant ages, I have fully understood them all.
"Throughout hundreds of thousands of births, you have diligently practiced various ascetic austerities;
whether the Buddha was present or had entered nirvāṇa, your vows were ever fulfilled.
He then addressed Akṣayamati:
I have grasped the infinite hundreds of thousands of past lives;
dwelling in the power of mastery, I now perceive them all clearly.
That you have accomplished the fruit of sainthood—I see it all manifest at this very moment.
Having grasped the inconceivable and the true nature of all conditioned phenomena,
you dwell before the Buddha and offer praise, making offerings to the Honored One among Two-Legged Beings.
Therefore, I now entreat you, the Dharma King of all the Sages.
"In the presence of the Buddha Samantaguhya-rāja, you grasped the most supreme vows;
having received the Buddha’s manifestation of supernormal powers, you have now attained this fruit.
Thus spoke the Bodhisattva Amoghadarśin to the Honored Muni:
“Regarding the various vows made throughout hundreds of thousands of births, how can they be grasped?
I pray that you will briefly explain them for me, so that I may attain understanding.
“Aśūnyapratibhāna! [The Buddha said:]”
In the past, he made this vow:
"When Raigarbha attains Buddhahood and is seen sitting beneath the Bodhi tree, I shall request him to preach the Dharma.
The former Buddha was named Keturāja, the World-Honored One of Universal Eye."
The common refuge for all sentient beings—
At that time, he made a vast vow, Seeking unsurpassed bodhi;
For the sake of the Tathāgata Sūryaprabha, He fashioned a great wheel of the seven precious jewels.
At that time, in that place, you already made the most supreme vow,
O Bodhisattva Amoghadarśin!
I know this vow entirely.
He constructed monasteries of the seven treasures, adorned with various colors,
to offer to the Sugata of the present and to bestow extensively upon the Buddhas of the future.
Having made this vow, he departed immediately.
The foremost among the assembly of Buddhas, the lion supreme among men,
named Acintya, the World-Honored One of Excellent Birth—
to him I offered a parasol of the seven precious gems, exquisitely adorned and most subtle.
The Great Sage, God among Gods, the Buddha with the Universal Eye,
having been honored with offerings of bright lamps, made this great vow at this place:
"In both recent and distant ages, there have been many Tathāgatas."
Trillions upon trillions, with numbers doubling even further,
in the presence of all these Buddhas, they have made immeasurable great vows,
so that all sentient beings may fully attain swift peace and happiness.
Before the Buddha Samantaguptarāja, he first gave rise to such a thought:
"I shall now recount for you how, in the past, you practiced until reaching Bodhi;
may all the great earth sprout every kind of flower."
At the abode of the Buddha Cloud-Thunder Sound, for the sake of benefiting the world,
he then made this vow:
"If there are any sentient beings who hear my name, may they all attain Buddhahood."
At the abode of the Buddha Indradhvaja, he presented a great and wondrous offering of precious jewels.
He further made these virtuous vows:
"If anyone beholds me with their eyes within this world, may they all attain Buddhahood."
In the presence of the Buddha Sūryaprabha, he offered a wheel of the seven treasures,
emitting immeasurable and vast flames of light, dazzling and most brilliantly beautiful.
Having further made his vow at that time, he vowed to be born in a buddha-field.
He adorned a monastery with the seven treasures, most elegant and of various colors;
because of these rare and extraordinary things, he offered them to the Sugata.
Having further made a vow, he obtained a wondrous celestial palace.
In this place of joy and delight, they all shall attain the path of Buddhahood.
At the presence of the Unsurpassed Tathāgata, that Lion-King among Men,
they offered precious jeweled canopies and made this most excellent vow:
"May all classes of sentient beings not be scorched by the sun;
may their bodies and minds find peace and happiness, free from the affliction of feverish distress.
Having offered lamps as an act of charity at the abode of the Sugata,"
He further made this great vow:
"May all sentient beings who eat meat at the place where my life ends attain the path of Buddhahood;
and may those who hear my name be free from greed and stinginess."
Even if one hears this within a dream, there shall be no thought of attachment or stinginess;
all shall attain the path of Buddhahood, with the sole exception of those who have already seen the Truth.
If anyone beholds you with their eyes, they shall be freed from all greed and envy.
Whether in dreams by day or night, you should likewise abandon all stained and stingy thoughts;
all shall attain Buddhahood, with the sole exception of those who have already seen the Truth.
Whether there be those who feel compassion for you, or those who give rise to hatred and jealousy—
In your presence, you shall become a Dharma King of the Buddhas. If,
at the time of your final passing, you again diligently seek awakening,
I now speak to you according to reality regarding your true merit.
"In a future age, may I surely attain this state of unsurpassed honor.
If there are any sentient beings— whether dwelling in water, on land,
or moving through the air— who eat the flesh of my body, may they all attain Buddhahood."
I already know that for the sake of bringing peace and happiness to sentient beings,
you have diligently cultivated the Bodhisattva path and fulfilled the practices throughout the great trichiliocosm.
Because sentient beings harbor many doubts and slander, you do not manifest yourself.
Such beings as these, at that very moment and in this very place,
if they should attain faith, right thought, and so forth, as well as a joyful mind,
shall all attain perfect enlightenment— except for those who have already seen the Truth.
If a person wishes to behold him who is honored and relied upon by the world,
or desires to see the turning of the wheel of Dharma, or seeks to alleviate the manifold sufferings of beings—
for such a person’s sake, one generates the mind [of awakening] for the benefit of bodhi.
If there are those who delight in making offerings to the Dharma Kings of the three periods of time,
or if people wish to give birth to a mass of all merits—
such sentient beings as these should uphold this samādhi.
At that time, having spoken these verses, the World-Honored One rose from his seat, returned to the monastery, and lay down on his right side in his usual quiet chamber.
