The Tathāgata Śākyamuni has attained immeasurable eloquence, the most unsurpassed eloquence, the eloquence that cannot be answered,
the eloquence free from attachment, the eloquence of supreme liberation, the unimpeded eloquence, the eloquence of perfected nature,
the eloquence of perfected teaching, the eloquence that bestows freedom from feverish distress, the eloquence regarding both the questioned and the unasked, and the eloquence of foreknowledge. If...
The eloquence of signs, the eloquence of signlessness, the eloquence of profound silence, the eloquence capable of removing anger,
the eloquence of various phrases and names, the eloquence of profound syllables and their exposition, the eloquence of expounding profound gentleness,
the eloquence of immeasurable analogies, the eloquence of no-questions-and-no-answers, and the eloquence fully endowed with meditative concentration.
...possessing vast eloquence, possessing inconceivable eloquence, possessing blossoming eloquence, possessing pure eloquence,
possessing indestructible eloquence, possessing eloquence that is wise and unimpaired, possessing eloquence with a mind free from attachment,
possessing eloquence with a mind free from stinginess, possessing eloquence that does not lose syllables or phrases, and possessing [eloquence] that is not stolen.
He possesses eloquence; he possesses the eloquence of non-delusive speech; he possesses the eloquence that fully develops the intent for preaching the Dharma;

he possesses the eloquence that fully preaches the Dharma to develop the pure mind from within afflictions; he possesses the eloquence that fully preaches by means of approaching [the audience] with chapters and verses;

he possesses the eloquence to fully speak of the past; he possesses the eloquence to fully speak of the future; he possesses the eloquence to fully speak of the present; he possesses the eloquence to fully speak of the marvelous.
“...eloquence, eloquence endowed with the supreme and wondrous wisdom of non-arising, and eloquence that brings joy to all the great assemblies.
At that time, Amoghadarśin spoke these verses:
“In the past, you have already with a sincere heart Made offerings to immeasurable Buddhas.”
Therefore, as the Honored One among men, you have now attained the Unsurpassed Way.
Through inconceivable roots of goodness, the Buddha has attained these manifold eloquences:
the incalculable various eloquences and the eloquence of unimpeded development.
The eloquence of unsurpassed liberation, the eloquence that accomplishes conversion,
the eloquence that extensively proclaims all marks, and the eloquence regarding questions asked or unasked;
the various explanations of the profound, and the eloquence that accords with analogies.
With pure and inconceivable voice, Possessing eloquence in wondrous exposition,
Accomplished in the purity of meaning, And possessing definitive eloquence regarding all marks;
Inconceivable and non-regressive, His eloquence is neither base nor inferior.
Excellent!
You do not lose a single word or phrase; with your non-delusive, gathered eloquence, you are able to sever the mind of afflictions; your eloquence never forgets the Ten Powers.
Supreme and proximate, proclaiming eloquence regarding the three times;
whether noble or non-noble, such is the conformable eloquence.
Without distance or birth, and so forth; near-hearing and far-reaching eloquence.
He speaks of the virtues of the Sugata with a voice that is clear, resonant, and eloquent.

Even if one were to take a single hair and draw from the waters of the great ocean, one might be able to know their number and cause them to dry up entirely; yet [the merit of his speech] cannot be measured.
There is no one who knows the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas’ great and supreme eloquence.
One might be able to measure the limits of space, or weigh Mount Sumeru to discern its exact weight; yet none can know this.
"The power of the Tathāgata’s wisdom and eloquence cannot be overcome by anyone;
even though one were to pass through countless eons, one could not fathom such eloquence as this.
At that time, Anagha (Amoghadarśin) again addressed Ānanda:

"Elder, you should know that the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, possess the great Brahma-voice; the lion’s voice; the heroic and courageous voice; the voice of the dragon king; the sound of strings and songs; the soft and beautiful voice; the sounds of small and large thunder; the inconceivable voice; the immeasurable and wondrous voice; the boundless and supreme voice; the perfect voice; the non-regressive voice; the kalaviṅka bird’s voice; the pure and joyful voice; the Tathāgata’s discriminating voice; the Tathāgata’s cognizant voice; the Tathāgata’s profound voice; the Tathāgata’s irreproachable voice; the Tathāgata’s unyielding voice; the Tathāgata’s crystal-clear voice; the undecaying and undiminished voice; the Tathāgata’s exquisite voice; the Tathāgata’s most excellent voice; and the Tathāgata’s voice that is never not excellent."

The Tathāgata is fully endowed with the voice of all-encompassing merit; it is said that in this regard, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, causes all sentient beings within a single world-system to hear with delight by means of a single sound, and again, by means of a single sound, causes the sentient beings within two world-systems to likewise desire to hear with delight; in this manner, from one sound up to hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of nayutas of boundless world-systems, the sentient beings therein likewise delight in hearing it.
The sentient beings there, hearing the voice of the Tathāgata, understand it thus and recognize it thus, all saying:
"The Tathāgata is preaching the Dharma for me."
"Thus it is, Ānanda!
The inconceivable voices of the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, are sounds that bring benefit.
Just as the orb of the sun illuminates Jambudvīpa, so do all sentient beings with eyes receive the benefit of wisdom."
"In this same way, Elder Ānanda, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha’s wheel of Dharma of voice is pure and subtle; his deliverance of all beings is likewise so."
It is like the fifteenth night of the first spring month, when the lunar disc is full, clear, and brightly shining, free from all clouds and veils.
The people of Jambudvīpa all go out to observe it, enjoying themselves to their heart's content, because of the moon’s full splendor.
In this way, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha’s wheel of Dharma is pure and subtle; that sentient beings obtain benefit is because they encounter the light of the Tathāgata’s Dharma.
“Venerable Ānanda!

It is just as all rivers, streams, brooks, and gullies—every water, whether great or small—enters the great ocean and all become of one taste; yet this single taste fully encompasses all various tastes.”
Furthermore, there are immeasurable and wondrous precious jewels; although humans and non-humans covet these treasures, the great ocean is so deep and vast that it is difficult to cross.

In this same way, the wheel of Dharma of the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha’s pure voice is difficult to understand, yet it enables all sentient beings to obtain the benefit of the Dharma-treasure and immeasurable peace and happiness—just so.
“Venerable Ānanda!

It is like the great earth, which opens up seeds and causes all things to grow; it benefits sentient beings with such abundance that there is no lack. Villages, cities, royal capitals, and all realms depend entirely upon this earth.”

In this same way, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, turns the wheel of Dharma with a voice that is pure and subtle; he rescues all immeasurable sentient beings, causing them all to rejoice, and it is likewise so.
“Venerable Ānanda!
Just as space is not obstructed by the coming and going of the world, yet this space provides comfort and security to all things;
so too, the wheel of Dharma of the voice of the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha—pure, subtle, and wondrous—is likewise beneficial to all.”
“Venerable Ānanda!

It is, for example, like the pārijātaka and kovidāra trees in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, whose flowers and leaves are in full bloom; when the devas go there to stroll and observe, there is none who is not delighted.”
"In this way, the Tathāgata’s wheel of Dharma through his voice clearly expounds the sounds of all phenomena; the nectar-like benefit and joy is likewise so.
At that time, Amoghadarśin spoke these verses:
"The World-Honored One’s Brahma-voice is the foremost in Jambudvīpa; The Tathāgata’s voice is pure and supreme, surpassing all other sounds."
The voice of a majestic lion, and the sound of a great dragon;
the harmonious and gentle tones of strings and flutes, inconceivable throughout the ten directions.
The thunderous roar of bells and drums, a boundless sound that vibrates everywhere.
The sound of a Buddha-land being fulfilled, the sound that never diminishes,
the voice of the kalaviṅka bird, the sound of loving compliance and joy,
the noble, joyful, and unclouded sound, and the sounds of instruction and non-instruction.
The sound of profound unconditionedness, the sound free from censure and slander;
the sound of words and syllables that are difficult to perceive yet well-discriminated;
the sound free from all decline, the beautiful and universally pervasive sound.
There is no sound of bondage, nor any sound of forgetfulness.
All sounds of merit are spoken by the Refuge of the World;
with a single voice, he can pervade all realms.
Taming the multitudes of sentient beings, they all joyfully delight in hearing [the teaching],
each saying:
"Now the Tathāgata is preaching the Dharma for me alone."
With a single voice, the Tathāgata reaches as far as worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges;
all sentient beings therein delight in hearing it.
It is like the emergence of radiant light, which illuminates all things.
The World-Honored One, with such a voice, expounds the Dharma for the multitude.
On the fifteenth day of early spring, the full moon is bright and pure;
like this orb of the bright moon, it shines everywhere upon Jambudvīpa.
Causing all to attain joy, their benefit is likewise boundless;
the Refuge of the World is like this moon—there is none who beholds it without delight.
With pure and wondrous sounds, he is able to bring benefit to all.
The most supreme in Jambudvīpa, it is inconceivable.
Like the great ocean, which is boundless and the source of all treasures,
deep and vast beyond easy crossing, it brings benefit to all beings.
The Great Victorious Buddha is thus; there is none superior to him.
Whether through manifest teaching or non-manifest [signs], his voice is exceedingly difficult to comprehend.
Pure and beyond reproach, he is able to bestow all happiness.
Within these three thousand worlds, all sentient beings are established;
such is the Buddha’s voice, benefiting beings in ways inconceivable.
Just as space is unobstructed and enables all manner of flight, so too does his voice pervade all.
The World-Honored One’s voice is thus, Broadly moistening all multitudes.
Like celestial fragrant flowers and trees, In full bloom, bringing sublime benefit;
So too the various voices of the Tathāgata, Perfectly endowed, benefit the world.
If I were to speak of the merits of the Buddha’s voice for the duration of an eon,
even after passing through a hundred eons, I could not fathom its beginning or its end;
so it is with all Buddhas— their voices are inconceivable.
If all sentient beings throughout the ten directions were to speak with boundless eloquence from many mouths,
they could not exhaust the limits of the Buddha’s merit in his voice;
such is the World-Honored One’s inconceivable sound.
Should all beings, whether of water or land,
Even if they were all to attain Buddhahood, They could not fathom the limits or depths of his voice;
Such are the Sugatas, with their inconceivable sounds.
Such a Tamer of Men has no equal in his voice;
if one can follow it with mindfulness, one will never fall into the evil realms.
If there are bodhisattvas who hear the Buddha’s perfect voice, [they shall likewise not fall].
"You shall become a King of the Buddha-Dharma with inconceivable voice.

At that time, the Four Heavenly Kings, Śakra-devānām-indra, the son of Yama, the son of Tuṣita, the son of Vaśavartin, as well as Maheśvara together with his son named Śreṣṭhidatta, Mahābrahmā, the gods of the Śuddhāvāsa heavens, and other gods of great power and majesty from both the Desire and Form Realms—including all the sons of the gods—having heard the description by the Bodhisattva Amoghadarśin of the merits of the Buddha’s voice, marveled at such an unprecedented occurrence. They scattered fine powdered sandalwood incense over the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Amoghadarśin and completed their offerings to him throughout the ten directions.
At that time, there were sixty billion hundred thousand nayutas of devas from the realms of desire and form who, upon hearing this sound, all planted the roots of goodness for unsurpassed bodhi;
five thousand bhikṣus also gave rise to the mind of unsurpassed bodhi and donned the armor of great vows;
and seven million bhikṣuṇīs gave rise to the unsurpassed mind and made great vows.
One hundred thousand upāsakas rose from their flower seats and approached the Great Bodhisattva Amoghadarśin;

furthermore, two billion nayutas of women each removed the jewels, gems, and necklaces from their bodies and offered them to the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Amoghadarśin, and likewise made great vows for unexcelled bodhi.

Chapter Six: Praising the Tathāgata’s Merits The *Bodhisattva-nien-fo-san-mei-jing* (Sutra on the Bodhisattva’s Samādhi of Mindfulness of the Buddha), Chapter Six: Praising the Tathāgata’s Merits. At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Amoghadarśin addressed Ānanda, saying:
“How marvelous! How extraordinary!”
How rare!

The Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, possess complete and profound knowledge of the coming and going within birth and death; they remember and recognize their places of birth, as well as their relatives and kinsmen, and they skillfully understand afflictions and all the faults and calamities of evil.

He was endowed with the primary and secondary marks of excellence; he was fully possessed of the practice of equanimity and great renunciation, as well as of morality, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation; he was complete in the six supernormal powers and had reached the further shore.

Whether it be loving-kindness or great loving-kindness, compassion or great compassion, sympathetic joy or great sympathetic joy, or equanimity or great equanimity—these are supreme and peerless, having reached the further shore.
In majestic deportment, supernormal powers, and all dharmas, he is most supreme and unimpeded, having reached the further shore.
Whether demonstrating what is possible or impossible to all directions, his benefit is most supreme, having reached the further shore.
Furthermore, he has attained the peerless excellence of śamatha and vipaśyanā, reaching the further shore.
He has also reached the further shore of all dhyānas, liberations, samādhis, and samāpattis, which are supreme and unsurpassed.

Free from greed, free from hatred, and free from delusion; free from pride, free from dullness, free from transgression, and free from the conceit of having transcended conceit; free from confusion and free from anger—having delivered beings from the five realms of existence and the four *vīśāradas* (or, as some say, the dharmas of giving and precepts), and being entirely without the sense of stinginess in the world, they possess the most supreme and peerless discourse on the roots of goodness of sentient beings and the theory of karmic retribution, reaching the further shore.
The aggregate of precepts of all sentient beings is uninterrupted, unblemished, and unturbid; it is unmixed and ineffable, characterized by wise clarity and purity, and is courageous and supreme.

Among śramaṇas, brahmins, humans, devas, māras, and Brahmās—the great lords of all worlds—there is not a single sentient being who can fathom even a hair’s breadth of the Tathāgata’s divisions of ethical discipline and meditative concentration; furthermore, there is no one at all who can surpass him.
Venerable sir, you should know that one should contemplate in this way:
"I may be able to reach the very limits of space, but I cannot measure the morality, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and knowledge-and-vision of the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones."
Why is this so? Because they are boundless.

The Tathāgata’s precepts, meditative concentration, supernormal powers, and all dharmas are not to be conceived by those of shallow understanding; they are profoundly unfathomable, and none can exhaustively fathom them.
Then, Akṣayamati spoke these verses:
“The World-Honored One has exhausted birth and death; Abiding in the womb is inconceivable.
Taking the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) as mother, There is nothing with which it can be compared.”
Fully endowed with virtuous merits, there is none in the world who can equal you;
your physical marks are the thirty-two primary signs and the eighty secondary refinements.
Inconceivable to the world, you have gathered all wholesome karmas.
How wonderful!
Honored One among Men, you are fully perfected in sublime transcendence.
Through relinquishment and great relinquishment, your mind is liberated from the afflictions.
The various supreme deeds of skillful means are fulfilled beyond compare. Fully endowed with precepts,
concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the analytical knowledge of liberation,
the qualities of all Buddhas are boundless, as they have reached the further shore of the six supernormal powers.
The Tathāgata, endowed with the practices of loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity,
is able to untie the bonds of sentient beings and deliver them from various sufferings.
The profound mass of wisdom of all Buddhas is inconceivable;
their majestic deportment is peerless, and their supernormal powers have reached the further shore.
Free from all afflictions, they are well-versed in the ultimate truth.
Whether in what is possible or what is impossible, they are fully endowed with benefit.
Their meditative concentration and liberation are thus inconceivable;
they are well-versed in śamatha, vipaśyanā, and the like.
Having reached that which does not exist in the world, forever free from all evil thoughts,
well-trained in concentration and liberation, he has eradicated the affliction of ignorance.
His pure precepts are unbroken, neither leaking nor turbid.
Having well studied the precepts without fail, he is a person of courage, vigor, clarity, and wisdom.
There is not a single sentient being— whether among śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, humans, devas, Māras, or Brahmās— who harbors doubt or a mind of slander.
With a heart of faith free from doubt, always skillfully training in purity;
though I may know the vast characteristics of the four directions of space,
I cannot fathom the courageous and unsurpassed pure precepts.
One might be able to blow upon the waters of the sea with a single breath and cause them to dry up completely,
yet one cannot fathom the Tathāgata’s pure Dharma, illumination, and precepts;
one might be able to blow upon Mount Sumeru with a single breath and reduce it to total fragments, yet [one cannot fathom the Tathāgata’s pure Dharma, illumination, and precepts].
Even the great and small Cakravāḍa mountains would be reduced to dust,
yet one could not fathom the limit of the Tathāgata’s pure precepts;
though one were to pass through kalpas numbering as many, one could never measure its extent.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Amoghadarśin thought to himself: "Excellent!

May the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha deign to exercise his majestic power and descend upon this assembly. I now wish, for the sake of all these bodhisattvas, to inquire of the Tathāgata regarding the Buddha-remembrance samādhi (buddhānusmṛti-samādhi)."
"World-Honored One, although you previously spoke their names in the midst of the great assembly, you did not elaborate upon them and instead entered your private chamber to lie on your right side.
At that time, the World-Honored One immediately knew his thought.
By the Buddha’s spiritual power, this trichiliocosm was shaken in six ways and underwent eighteen transformations.

As previously described, he emitted a great radiance that universally illuminated this Sahā world; the light of the sun, moon, stars, the various devas of the desire realm, and the boundless Brahmās as numerous as the sands of the Ganges was all eclipsed and no longer appeared, while only the Buddha’s divine light shone with extraordinary brilliance.
Out of compassion for sentient beings, he rose from his reclining position, adjusted his robes, and proceeded to the place of the great assembly.

At that time, the various people of the world, devas, śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, and asuras each beheld the Tathāgata’s extraordinary radiance as he rose from his flower seat and approached the Buddha's presence; they paid homage with palms joined and withdrew to stand to one side.
At that time, Amoghadarśin saw from afar the Buddha approaching, his countenance serene and majestic, his deportment composed and orderly, and his marks and signs of excellence fully perfected.
Having seen this, he addressed the Elder Ānanda:

"The World-Honored One is now coming from his quiet chamber; he will surely expound and reveal the most supreme and foremost Truth (paramārtha-satya), which is free from false speech, skillfully proclaimed, and beyond conceptual discrimination."

They are well able to reflect and do not give rise to evil karma; their physical actions are without transgression, their verbal actions are without reproach, and their mental actions are without failure—the three karmas are all pure.
He is fully endowed with morality, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation;
he possesses supreme skillful means, supernormal powers, benefits, and inconceivable, extraordinary eloquence;

he thoroughly understands birth and death such that none can surpass him; his dwelling in the womb is pure, his maternal lineage is noble and eminent, and he is most fully endowed with all virtues and merits.
He is endowed with inconceivable marks and embellishments;
he is endowed with the causes and conditions of the past as well as his mental resolve;
and through liberation from afflictions, his mind is fully perfected.
If one relinquishes through great relinquishment, transcendence is fully accomplished;
if the five consciousnesses are without grasping, freedom from defilement is fully accomplished;
and the fivefold Dharma-body is pure and fully accomplished.
Having ultimately reached the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*) and the characteristics of all phenomena and their true nature (*dharmatā*), they have reached the other shore;
having reached the other shore in *vipaśyanā* and *śamatha*, the faculties (*indriya*), powers (*bala*), factors of awakening (*bodhyaṅga*), and the path (*mārga*);
and having reached the other shore in inconceivable loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity, as well as in profound shame and remorse (*hrī-apatrāpya*).
Having already reached the further shore of mastery over all phenomena, they fully know and see all phenomena of the past, future, and present, remaining unattached and non-retrogressive.
He is able to know all past bodily actions and also knows their transformations, having reached the other shore;
his verbal and mental actions are likewise so.
"Elder Ānanda!
"The Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, can in a single thought-moment know the mental activities and the good and evil of all sentient beings; there is nothing he does not fully comprehend.
At that time, Anagata-darśin addressed Ānanda, saying:
"It is like the great ocean, deep and vast, difficult to cross;"
The ocean-like profundity and vastness of the Buddhas' aggregate of ethical discipline (*śīla-skandha*) is likewise so.
Just as Mount Sumeru can never be toppled,
the Tathāgata’s aggregate of meditative concentration (*samādhi-skandha*) is similarly imperturbable.
"Elder Ānanda!
Just as space is pure and all-encompassing, without limit;
so too do the samādhis of the Buddhas encompass the boundless categories of pure wisdom and gather the pure minds of all sentient beings."
“Venerable Ānanda!
Just as the light of the sun can illuminate all immeasurable forms and images,
so too does the Dharma-light of the Tathāgata illuminate everything, leaving no darkness unlit.”
"Elder Ānanda! Just as a great fire consumes mountains, forests, and all manner of things,
so too can the Dharma-fire of the Tathāgata burn away the immeasurable afflictions of sentient beings, enabling them to attain eternal purity."
“Venerable Ānanda!
It is like a gushing spring that overflows and forms a deep pool outside, capable of washing all things and making them pure;
likewise, the Dharma-water of the Tathāgata removes all fetters and burdens of sentient beings, enabling them to constantly attain peace.”
“Venerable Ānanda!
Just as a king of physicians skillfully treats the various ailments of sentient beings,
so too does the Dharma-medicine of the Tathāgata eliminate the grave illnesses of birth and death for sentient beings, causing them all to be removed forever.”
"Elder Ānanda! Just as the seasonal rain nourishes and benefits the grasses and trees, causing them all to grow;
so too does the Dharma-rain of the Tathāgata nourish all withered sentient beings."
“Venerable Ānanda!
Just as the lion’s roar causes all wild beasts to cower and submit,
so too can the Dharma-sound of the Tathāgata destroy those sentient beings who cling to the view of a self, causing them to be forever liberated from it.”
“Venerable Ānanda!
Just as a great ship can carry one across to the other shore,
so too does the Tathāgata’s Dharma-ship ferry all sentient beings to the further shore beyond the four currents.”
“Venerable Ānanda!
Just as the udumbara flower is rare and difficult to see,
so too is the appearance of a Tathāgata in the world difficult to encounter.”
"Venerable Ānanda!
Just as when the flowers of the pārijātaka and tārā trees are in full bloom, their fragrance is exceptionally sublime;
so too does the radiance of the Great Man’s marks shine forth."
“Venerable Ānanda!
Just as parents are able to nurture their children,
so too is the Tathāgata, skillfully benefiting sentient beings.”
“Venerable Ānanda!
If someone were to say:
‘The Tathāgata has appeared in the world; his correct teaching is boundless.’”
This is called speaking truthfully.
If someone were to say:
"The Tathāgata appears in the world and speaks inconceivable eloquence," [that would be so].
"This is called the correct exposition. Elder Ānanda!

Briefly stated, the Tathāgata possesses boundless eloquence, unattached eloquence, unimpeded eloquence, supremely liberated eloquence, accomplished sublime eloquence, ever-conforming eloquence, progressively approaching eloquence, eloquence whether questioned or unasked, subtle and pure eloquence, supreme eloquence, the eloquence of great loving-kindness, the eloquence of great compassion, the eloquence of great sympathetic joy, the eloquence of great equanimity, the eloquence of a Buddha’s appearance in the world, and furthermore, the eloquence of benefiting others."
Venerable Ānanda!
If someone were to say:
"The Tathāgata appears in the world fully endowed with the benefit of all sentient beings."
This is called the correct teaching.
Elder Ānanda!
If someone were to say:
"Sentient beings have no peace, no rescue, no refuge, no resort, and no master; when the Tathāgata appears in the world, he is able to provide them with peace, rescue, refuge, resort, and a master."
This is called the correct teaching.
"Venerable Ānanda!

If I were to spend an eon, or even up to a hundred eons, proclaiming the merits, wisdom, and eloquence of the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, my speech would not equal even one-hundred-millionth part of them."

Furthermore, even if one were to proclaim and describe the merits and eloquence of the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha throughout immeasurable and all-encompassing kalpas, one could never reach their limit.
“Elder Ānanda!
Suppose there were a person who was frail, aged, and afflicted with lameness and deformity, staying in another’s house, and said to that person:
‘How wonderful, O noble sir!’”
"Although I am such a person, I can take all the immeasurable waters with a single hair-tip, place them within my mouth, and cause them all to dry up.
If this man possesses neither supernormal powers nor incantations, would he be credible in being able to perform such a feat?
Ānanda replied,
“This is difficult to believe.
Amoghadarśin said:
"Truly, it cannot be done; it would be mere empty words.
Thus it is, Ānanda!
I say that the merits and eloquence of the Buddhas cannot be exhausted, just as that man has no way to exhaust the water."
“Venerable Ānanda!
Even if I were to spend hundreds of thousands of millions of nayutas of kalpas, I could not proclaim even a single hair’s breadth of the merits, wisdom, and eloquence of the Buddhas;
only a Buddha and a Buddha can fully exhaust them.”
“Venerable Ānanda!

Just as this great earth accommodates sentient beings—whether they have feet or are footless, four-footed or many-footed, with form or formless, with perception, without perception, or neither with nor without perception; whether in this world or other worlds, in a thousand worlds, a hundred thousand worlds, or in all immeasurable and boundless worlds—the sentient beings therein shall all attain Buddhahood.”
Even if these World-Honored Ones were to speak of the Buddha’s merits for hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of kalpas, they could not exhaust even a single hair’s breadth of them.
Such merits are fully possessed without exception.
Then, Amoghadarśin spoke these verses:
“O Elder Ānanda!
From there the Dharma King has come; among all the multitudes of the world, there are none who do not offer him worship.”
Lord of Supreme Radiance, whose merits are all innumerable,
you who speak of the most supreme benefit, the true speech, the unborn speech,
the truthful speech, the non-deceptive speech, the peerless and excellent speech.
He utters subtle and wondrous sounds, The Great Wise One skillfully proclaims the teaching.
Body, speech, and mind are pure; He does not give rise to thoughts of any evils.
The Tathāgata’s supreme morality, concentration, Foremost wisdom, and liberation—
His knowledge and vision of liberation, etc., and his majestic deportment are ever inconceivable.
His unsurpassed supernormal powers and wisdom bring benefit beyond compare;
he has perfectly attained stainless conduct and the most supreme, subtle eloquence.
The Unsurpassed Honored One among Men, Fully knowing birth and death,
His dwelling in the womb was peerless, And so too was his maternal lineage.
With inconceivable and extraordinary marks, And eighty kinds of subtle excellences,
His countenance was most distinguished, Elegant and peerless in its symmetry.
He possessed a mind free from delusion; In renunciation, he was likewise great.
Transcending all desires, The five consciousnesses were fully present.
His realized wisdom transcends the six supernormal powers;
He is fully endowed with the four analytical knowledges and possesses immeasurable knowledge and vision.
His inconceivable manifold miraculous transformations, And his śamatha and vipaśyanā, have all reached the further shore.
The Lord who has attained the relinquishing of defilements, Whose majestic deportment is ever sovereign,
A great divine king among the assembly, Advancing slowly from that place;
The Unattached Sugata, Abiding in the wisdom of the ten powers.
Practicing loving-kindness and radiating the light of the Dharma, as taught by the One of All-Surpassing Wisdom:
one may know the measure of the waters of the great ocean— its boundless depth and vast extent—
but one cannot fathom the limits of the unsurpassed power of purity, ethical discipline, and meditative concentration.
Though one were to pass through billions of kalpas, one could not know its limit;
even if one were to take Mount Sumeru in hand and hurl it up to the Brahma Heaven,
one could not disturb the Tathāgata’s primordial, most profound samādhi.
One might roam through empty space and know its boundaries;
yet no one can measure the Tathāgata’s indestructible wisdom.
One might even tread upon the void with one's feet and exhaust its limits; [but the Buddha’s wisdom remains unfathomable].
Unable to fathom his freedom from defilement, the World-Honored One who has cast off all burdens is like the sun that dispels darkness, allowing all forms, good and evil, to be seen;
as the natural Teacher of the world, he is able to extinguish the gloom of ignorance.
Just as when the moon is full, all beings rejoice;
so too, upon beholding the King of Dharma-Light, all who see him are filled with joy.
Like lighting a bright lamp at night, those with eyes cannot fail to see it.
The Peerless Lamp of Subduing, who can manifest the radiance of the Dharma;
the World Teacher, the Torch of the Dharma-Lamp, who skillfully extinguishes all aggregates and proclaims the self-arisen Dharma, which is heard everywhere by sentient beings.
The Greatly Wise and Supreme King of Physicians is like a gushing spring;
with the medicine of the Dharma, he eliminates all ailments and can bestow all happiness.
He is like the Great Dragon King, who universally rains down ambrosia.
It causes this great earth to be entirely moistened;
The World-Honored One of Great Compassion, His rain of Dharma is likewise.
Just as when the lion roars, All crawling creatures are struck with fear;
The Tathāgata resounds the sound of the Dharma, subduing all non-Buddhists.
Like a great sturdy ship, he is able to transport all;
the Buddha delivers many billions of beings, ferrying them to the shore beyond the four torrents.
Just as the udumbara flower is wondrously called rare,
so too is the Honored One among Men difficult to encounter— indeed, even more so than that.
He is the place of constant refuge for all the worlds.
Like the celestial city Sudarśana, where the pārijātaka flowers bloom in profusion,
radiating brilliant light— the place where the gods sport and delight—
the Refuge of the World surpasses them, for his marks and signs are exceedingly subtle and wondrous.
The World-Honored One has already manifested various supernatural transformations for my sake;
I shall now briefly proclaim the merits of all Buddhas.
By means of the deeds I have cultivated, I shall bestow benefit upon sentient beings.

Chapter Seven: The Tathāgata’s Supernatural Power Proving the True Teaching. *The Bodhisattva’s Samādhi of Mindfulness of the Buddha Sūtra*, Chapter Seven: The Tathāgata’s Supernatural Power Proving the True Teaching. At that time, the World-Honored One stroked the crown of the head of the Bodhisattva Amoghadarśin with his golden hand, extended his broad and long tongue, and addressed him, saying:
“Excellent, excellent!
"O Aśūnyadarśin, you have well spoken of the true merits of the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha; we believe what you have said.
Furthermore, O Aśūnyadarśin!"
If someone were to say:

"There are sentient beings who have no peace, no rescue, no refuge, no destination, and no lord; the Tathāgata, appearing in the world, is able to act as peace, rescue, refuge, destination, and lord for such sentient beings."
This is called the correct teaching.
Furthermore, Aśūnyadarśin!
If someone were to say:
“The Tathāgata appears in the world to preach inconceivable eloquence and boundless eloquence.
This is called the correct teaching.
Furthermore, Anavaśya!
If someone were to say:
"All sentient beings are deeply attached to greed, anger, and wrong views; when the Tathāgata appears in the world, he is able to completely eliminate these diseases of greed and the rest."
This is called the correct teaching.
Furthermore, Āśūnyaprekṣin!
If someone were to say:
"All sentient beings are defiled and attached by the stains of envy and jealousy; when the Tathāgata appears in the world, he causes them all to be completely severed.
This is called the correct teaching.
Furthermore, Amoghadarśin!
If someone were to say:

"All sentient beings lack a sense of shame and a dread of blame, yet when a Tathāgata appears in the world, he can cause sentient beings to become fully endowed with shame and dread of blame," this is called the correct teaching.
Furthermore, Āśūnya-darśin!
If someone were to say:
"All sentient beings are deeply attached to stinginess and pride; when the Tathāgata appears in the world, he is able to completely sever these, so that they are without stinginess or pride."
"This is called the correct teaching.
Furthermore, Āśūnyadarśin!
If someone were to say: "

"All sentient beings lack loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity, and harbor unwholesome, evil thoughts; when the Tathāgata appears in the world, he causes them all to be fully endowed with the four immeasurable minds and beneficial, wholesome thoughts."
This is called the correct teaching.
Furthermore, Āśūnyaprekṣin!
If someone were to say:
"All sentient beings lack all roots of goodness; the Tathāgata appears in the world to teach and transform them all, causing them to plant seeds of wholesome karma.
This is called the correct teaching.
Furthermore, Āśūnyadarśin!
If someone were to say:
"In this world of the five turbidities, where the illnesses of sentient beings increase, the Tathāgata appears in the world and is able to bring peace and happiness."
"What this person says is precisely what I have taught.
Why is this? Because I have appeared in this degenerate age to preach the Dharma for the benefit of all sentient beings."

At that time, when the Tathāgata touched the crown of the head of the Bodhisattva Amoghadarśin, in a single moment of thought, the sentient beings of this world, sustained by the Buddha’s spiritual power, all beheld the infinite, boundless, and incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) Buddhas in the pure lands of the eastern direction, and they heard the sounds of those Buddhas preaching the Dharma;
likewise, from the southern direction up to the ten directions, as clearly as seeing an *āmala* fruit in the palm of one's hand, all sentient beings beheld those pure Buddha-fields.

Furthermore, in the space of a single thought-moment, the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, stroked the crown of the head of the Bodhisattva Amoghadarśin with his golden hand. Through the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power, he manifested the most supreme vow-power of the past, whereby [Amoghadarśin] immediately beheld the Buddhas who had already entered parinirvāṇa in the pure Buddha-fields of the zenith, numbering in the measureless, boundless, and incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) hundreds of thousands of millions of billions.
Furthermore, by the power of upholding this samādhi, one is able to see all the Buddhas of the future.

At that time, Amoghadarśin, having beheld the various Buddhas, rose from his seat, adjusted his robes, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms in reverence, and addressed the World-Honored Buddha in verse:
"The waters of the trichiliocosm, A person might know their limit; But the number of Buddhas yet to come, No one can fathom."
The World-Honored One, the skillful tamer, possesses an immeasurable collection of precepts;
even if one were to contemplate them for vast eons, one could not fathom their limit.
It is as if there were a valiant hero who, with a single breath, causes Mount Sumeru to tremble.
When the Buddha enters the first dhyāna concentration, he cannot be moved for a thousand kalpas.
He walks upon the void and wanders through space;
one might be able to know its limits and measure, yet even throughout the exhaustion of all kalpas, one could never fathom the Buddha’s wisdom.
Space is formless and measureless, yet even a raging wind can move it;
the World-Honored One is free from afflictions, and none can sever his eloquence.
Like the sun shining upon space, its radiance is most brilliant and penetrating.
The majestic radiance of the Great Seer eclipses all else;
like the moon among the stars, his perfect halo is most delightful.
Thus, this King of the Dharma Moon is one toward whom all turn in reverence.
Just as the udumbara flower is rare in this world,
so too is it exceedingly difficult to encounter the Tamer of Men, the God among Gods. Now,
the Great Holy Honored One, out of compassion, has caressed the crown of my head.
Golden-hued and adorned with a hundred blessings, compassionate and benefiting all,
deeply understanding the true reality and fully endowed with merit;
the Refuge of the World speaks excellently, the supreme among those who discourse.
He proclaims an inconceivable sound, heard throughout the realms of the ten directions.
The Self-Existent Honored One, mindful with compassion, strokes the crown of my head with his hand;
thus I behold as many Most Victorious Kings of the World as there are grains of sand in the Ganges.
The Great Sage among men, with a single thought, touched the crown of my head;
I beheld all Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, just like Amitābha.
The Honored One among devas, for the benefit [of beings], with a single thought, touched the crown of my head.
May I behold the Immovable Realm and Akṣobhya, the Honored One among bipeds;
may he, the sphere of great compassion, touch my crown with his hand in a single thought.
May I behold the Buddha who has attained parinirvāṇa, the Teacher of all worlds.
The sphere of activity of great compassion, wherein the senses are well-subdued;
by the power of my former vows, at the very moment of being touched upon the crown of my head,
I beheld the future Buddhas, Maitreya and the other Refuges of the World.
As he touched the crown of my head, I beheld the Buddhas of the past and also saw the inconceivable Honored Ones of the ten directions who will appear in the future;
the Honored One, the Tamer with Buddha-eyes, immediately touched the crown of my head.
Furthermore, by virtue of past sublime vows, one is able to behold this pure land.
The Tathāgata’s inconceivability and his supernormal powers are likewise so;
his wisdom, meditative concentration, and all other merits are all beyond measure.
Out of compassion, the World-Honored One, In pity, looked upon me and taught me.
With his golden-colored hand, the Tathāgata Stroked the crown of my head;
I beheld the Buddhas of the ten directions, And golden stupas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
Furthermore, they see throughout the worlds of the ten directions countless Tathāgatas;
with most excellent stupas made of silver, adorned in various colors,
and with hundreds of thousands of musical performances, they constantly make offerings without ceasing.
I also see other lands, where the stupas of the Buddhas and their various requisites are made of gold,
silver, and crystal; each is one yojana high,
so upright, majestic, and exquisitely refined that they cannot be described in words.
He beheld the stupas of the Munis, adorned with various kinds of the seven treasures,
abiding in the midst of space, with celestial flowers strewn all around;
he further saw a most excellent stupa, twelve yojanas in height.
I beheld the Buddha Dīpaṃkara, whose pure light illumines all lands;
I further saw, in every place, inconceivable numbers of stupas;
and I beheld other supreme Honored Ones, who stroked the crown of my head with their hands.
With his soft and supple hand, the Buddha stroked the crown of my head in a single thought;
I beheld those Tathāgatas dwelling peacefully in their respective lands,
or else manifesting various forms within the sky.
Furthermore, I behold various bodhisattvas who have not yet escaped the burden of manifold delusions;
dwelling in immeasurable buddha-fields, they practice all manner of ascetic austerities,
constantly diligent in heart day and night, in their quest for supreme enlightenment.
Furthermore, I see in every place countless bodhisattvas who are constantly able to perform various acts of benefit for sentient beings;
they burn their bodies to emit radiance, seeking the causes and conditions for the Way.
Furthermore, I see various bodhisattvas dwelling peacefully before the Buddhas,
making offerings to the Buddhas who have entered parinirvāṇa at immeasurable, wondrous stupas,
seeking the benefit of awakening as well as great majestic power.
Beholding the conditions of the ten directions, They burn their bodies like the wick of a lamp;
Day and night they constantly cultivate the mind, Never flagging even for the sake of eating or resting.
Furthermore, they see the various bodhisattvas Relinquishing kingdoms, cities, wives, and children.
The head, eyes, marrow, and brain— For the sake of bringing peace and happiness to sentient beings,
I have seen all of these within them; The World-Honored One with Universal Eyes possesses sovereign power, Which cannot be fully expressed in words.
As I know it, he is the most supreme in the world.
When the God among Gods compassionately stroked the crown of my head with his hand,
I immediately beheld that assembly and took refuge in the Honored One among Men.

Chapter Eight: The Chapter on the Exhortation of Amoghadarśin. In the *Bodhisattva-nien-fo-san-mei-jing*, Chapter Eight: The Chapter on the Exhortation of Amoghadarśin. At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Amoghadarśin addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
The Tathāgata has remained in his chamber in tranquil seclusion for a long time, and this great assembly all yearns for him with longing.
The seats have now been fully prepared; we only pray that the World-Honored One, out of compassion for all beings, will deign to take this seat.
Then, Amoghadarśin adjusted his robes, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and said:
"World-Honored One!
I now wish to ask a question; I pray that you will briefly explain it, for I shall listen with a sincere heart and put it into practice."
The Buddha told Akṣayamati: "Ask whatever you wish;
I shall resolve your doubts and bring you joy, such that all devas and people of the world shall likewise bear witness."
Then, Akṣayamati addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
By practicing and cultivating which samādhi do bodhisattva-mahāsattvas come to see the joy of the Dharma and increase their minds?"

The samādhi he has heard is as vast as the great ocean, and his bodhicitta is as stable as Mount Sumeru; it cannot be moved by the heterodox winds of external paths, and his mind remains unattached even toward unimpeded dharmas.
Like space, it is unstained;
in shattering the darkness of ignorance, it is like the morning sun;
in bestowing the light of the Dharma, it is like the full moon.
It burns away all the aggregates with blazing, fierce flames, a great mass of fire that incinerates all afflictions.
It is like the rivers, oceans, and all waters, upon which all creatures of the watery realm depend for their livelihood.
Furthermore, it is like a great ship that can ferry one to the other shore;
it is also like a bridge that enables sentient beings not to fall into the swift current of birth-and-death and afflictions.
It is just as the pārijātaka tree produces all manner of sentient beings, and its seven flowers of awakening thoroughly permeate the worlds of the ten directions.
It is like the udumbara flower, rare in the world;
it is also like a skilled physician who effectively cures all ailments, providing vast salvation through great compassion and administering medicine according to the disease;
it is like a sandalwood tree that can eliminate the torment of heat.
"Furthermore, it is like a great rain that moistens and bestows upon all.
The flavor of the sublime Dharma is like fragrant honey; it causes the multitude to be fearless, just like the lion king."
They bring peace and happiness to sentient beings beyond that of a compassionate mother;
they deeply understand the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), master the characteristics of their meanings and implications, and attain skillful means regarding those meanings;
the same applies to the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*).

Skilled in the true path and endowed with expedient means, he expounds the Dharma according to reality, attaining the ability to bring peace and stability to the assembly and revealing the root source of sentient beings' birth and death.
The nature of all phenomena is of a single flavor like the ocean; his samādhi is as tranquil as the king of mountains; and his resolve for the Way is immovable, like the banner of Indra.
He attains firm and steadfast power; his physical form is upright and majestic, his deportment is complete, and he is free from all defilement;
his lineage is noble and eminent, and his merits are fully perfected.

They have attained boundless eloquence, unattached eloquence, eloquence of non-differentiated phrases, inconceivable eloquence, immeasurable eloquence, eloquence of profound liberation, accomplished supreme eloquence, ever-patient eloquence, progressively approaching eloquence, eloquence regarding questions and non-questions, indestructible eloquence, non-regressive eloquence, eloquence in various explanations of profound phrases and syllables, eloquence in profoundly and extensively expounding chapters, sections, and syllables, and eloquence in infinite and boundless parables and similes; all such qualities as these they fully possess.

May those who have not yet attained the Way cause them to attain it; may they obtain the Brahma-voice, the voice of mental joy, the voice of the kalaviṅka bird, the lion’s roar, and other sounds such as those of the great dragon, the bull king, the bell, and the drum; may they possess the beautiful voices of song, stringed instruments, and thunder; may they receive offerings from all the world, be endowed with the six supernormal powers (ṣaḍabhijñā) and reach the further shore, attain the dharma of non-forgetfulness and retention, and acquire all roots of goodness, dignified deportment, and proper conduct.
Then, Amoghadarśin asked in verse:
“O you of golden hue, adorned with a hundred blessings, who deeply understands the ultimate truth,
and who out of compassion brings benefit and peace— listen as I question the Buddhas.”
What samādhi should one cultivate to be fully endowed with pure merit,
to become a peerless Honored One among men, and to possess wisdom beyond reproach?
I now ask the World-Honored One, the most supreme and unsurpassed Lord.
By practicing which samādhi do they attain inconceivable merit?
How do the bodhisattvas become the most excellent among men?
One should diligently cultivate and practice the most supreme, tranquil concentration.
Having practiced this samādhi, how does one bring benefit to the world?
How does one attain spontaneity and become as vast in learning as the great ocean?
How does one obtain immovability and profound, wondrous wisdom?
Abiding in all the virtues of a Buddha, like a mountain that turns the wheel—
how is it that the mind is unattached, naturally like space,
subduing all non-Buddhists, and never giving rise to an evil thought?
How should one practice so as to become like the sun and the moon?
Furthermore, how should one act to be equal to that great torch?
What samādhi should one seek and cultivate so that its radiance illuminates all things?
How can the afflictions of aging and sickness in sentient beings be eliminated?
How can all beings be enabled to cross over the ocean of suffering?
How may one resolve to generate the bodhicitta and pay homage to the Honored One of the Three Realms?
How can they be compared to celestial flowers, Whose marks and signs are most brilliantly manifest?
The udumbara blooms but once in an age; Is it not even more difficult than this to encounter a Buddha?
How can they be compared to a King of Physicians, Who dispenses medicine to extinguish all maladies?
How does one well-subdue the sense faculties and dwell securely in the categories of ethical discipline?
How is it that, like a Dharma King, one transcends boundless merit?
How does one perceive the fulfillment of the Dharma, as if it were sweet and pure honey?
How does one possess the lion’s voice to bestow benefit upon sentient beings?
How is it that one is like a compassionate mother, bestowing inconceivable happiness upon the multitude?
How does one attain the four analytical knowledges and practice the most profound bodhi?
For my sake, speak of the most excellent, the unsurpassed, and the foremost path.
How can one attain and explain the great wisdom that is free from attachment?
How does one achieve skill in meaning and expedient means, and attain the inconceivable Dharma?
How does one skillfully know the characteristics of expedient means, and how does one know mundane and supramundane dharmas?
How can one attain the realization of the meaning,
and how further attain the Path?
How does one attain mindfulness?
How does one achieve perfect composure?
How does one become learned, with depth and breadth like the great ocean?
How are the true merits of all Buddhas described?
How are sentient beings described, the very source and root of birth and death?
How are all phenomena described as having no distinct characteristics, like the ocean which has but a single flavor?
How does one attain samādhi, immovable like the king of mountains,
with a mind of bodhi peaceful and tranquil, like the banner of Śakra?
How does one attain all other inconceivable states of bodhi?
How does one attain physical excellence and achieve all dignified deportments?
How does one attain birth in a noble lineage and become a Dharma King of merit?
How does one attain boundlessness and the eloquence of non-attachment?
How can one achieve accomplishment in the meaning of inconceivable phrases and syllables?
I pray that the Refuge of the World will explain this to me in detail.
How does one attain that which is most excellent, unsurpassed, and beyond compare?
As well as the teaching of non-attachment, freedom from fault, and patience;
approaching the inconceivable, whether there is questioning or no questioning;
the Brahma-sound, the sound of noble intention, and the excellent, wondrous voice of the kalaviṅka bird.
How can one practice the bodhisattva conduct?
I pray that the Honored One will instruct me.
How can one obtain the voice of a lion, a great dragon, and a bull king?
How does one obtain the sound of a bell, the melody of stringed song, and beautiful tones?
How does one attain wisdom?
I pray that the World-Honored One, the Tamer, will explain this.
How can one preach the Dharma with a mind that is never weary or satisfied,
without disparaging any virtues, and always emitting a voice like the roar of thunder?
How should one proclaim the various kinds of most profound teachings?
What are the various parables? How does one skillfully speak of the six supernormal powers?
How does one not lose the Dharma, maintaining mindfulness for hundreds of thousands of years, practicing diligently without weariness?
[How does one attain] the Universal Eye of the Honored One of wholesome dharmas?
If, for the sake of the worlds of the ten directions, you explain the cultivation of the inconceivable,
those who have no doubt regarding all wisdom will take refuge in it and seek liberation.
For this reason, on this very day, I inquire of the Tathāgata.

Then, by the power of his effortless miraculous activity (*anabhisaṃskāra-ṛddhi*), the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Amoghadarśin caused a celestial, wondrous jewel canopy—adorned with the seven precious gems and of various exquisite beauties—to spontaneously manifest in the sky directly above the World-Honored One.

Within this canopy, a rain of various flowers fell; they circled the Buddha three times and remained above his head, the blossoms inclining with reverence toward the World-Honored One. Then, from within the flowers, these verses were spoken:
"I take refuge in the Great Sage, The Perfectly Awakened One, the Honored One among two-legged beings."
"Neither among the devas nor among the people of the world is there anyone who can equal him.
At that time, these flowers fell upon the Buddha’s feet and then rose up again.
Having risen, they naturally scattered throughout the trichiliocosm.
Furthermore, from within the canopies, powdered sandalwood rained down, swirling through the air and falling upon the Buddha.
In an instant, they suddenly vanished, yet their fragrant scent remained rich and pervasive, filling the great trichiliocosm.
When these sentient beings smell this fragrance, their bodies and minds become peaceful and secure, and they all attain happiness, just as a bodhisattva attains the bliss of the four dhyānas.
Having manifested his supernatural powers, Akṣayamati then addressed the Buddha, saying:
"How does a bodhisattva attain great wisdom, swift wisdom, sharp wisdom, signless wisdom, profound wisdom, vast wisdom, universal wisdom, and fearless wisdom?"
How does one obtain unsurpassed roots of goodness, with a mind like a vajra that destroys all marks of phenomena;
with body and mind supple and pliant, and a mind as vast as the ocean;
with the categories of precepts immeasurable, and a mind like a massive boulder?
Their minds are gentle and supple, upright and dignified;
their minds are like the king of mountains, encompassing all wholesome dharmas;
their minds are like the great earth, able to bring peace to all.
One attains non-reliance on others and refrains from censuring the faults of others;
one attains the conduct leading to happy rebirths and dwells securely in all dharmas;
one proceeds correctly toward the unsurpassed World-Honored One and does not slander him.
In every birth, may they always attain the vision of Buddhas without separation;
while dwelling in this world, may they see the immeasurable Buddhas of other directions, hear the Dharma, and encounter the Sangha?
Furthermore, may they be able to take hold of pure lands, constantly cultivate roots of goodness, and achieve both self-benefit and the benefit of others?
For this reason, I now inquire of the World-Honored One.
For the sake of liberation and the benefit of sentient beings; for the sake of all bodhisattvas attaining the inconceivable and being fully endowed with roots of goodness, I inquire of the Tathāgata;
and because I have donned the great armor of *saṃnāha* (vows) to endure suffering out of compassion for all, I inquire of the Tathāgata.

For the sake of benefiting and bringing happiness to all sentient beings, I have donned the armor of the great vow; yet, while desiring to deliver them from birth and death, I harbor no notion of "sentient beings. Constantly benefiting sentient beings in this manner, I now inquire of the Tathāgata.
“World-Honored One!

Toward all sentient beings, I do not give rise to a mind of malice, nor do I harbor thoughts of anger, abuse, slander, revilement, or contempt. From the beginning, I have been free from resentment, hostility, or spite; I am without forgetfulness or confusion of mind, nor am I jealous. I harbor no bitter venom, but practice loving-kindness and compassion.”
Training myself in the Mahāyāna according to such characteristics, I inquire of the Tathāgata for the sake of benefiting others.
World-Honored One!

For the sake of sentient beings now, I renounce the pleasures of the five desires, am able to endure all sufferings, and bestow all happiness, acting as the light of the Dharma for all sentient beings.
“World-Honored One!

Regarding all internal and external phenomena, my mind is free from stinginess. Because I seek to benefit sentient beings through such qualities as these, I ask the Tathāgata this question, World-Honored One.”

I have now donned the armor of the great vow; for the sake of even a single sentient being, I would enter the great hells throughout kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges to undergo all manner of suffering and affliction, yet I have never, for even a single moment, allowed my unsurpassed bodhicitta to falter or be lost.
Therefore, for the sake of benefiting sentient beings, I am now able to endure immeasurable and extreme suffering without ever retreating from the mind of enlightenment.
For the sake of all beings, I ask the Tathāgata this question.
Having now donned such armor of the great vow, I act as a servant for all sentient beings; for their benefit, I ask the Tathāgata this question.
World-Honored One!
"For the sake of sentient beings, I now renounce my head, eyes, marrow, and brain; I endure all such sufferings without retreating from Bodhi.
It is regarding these circumstances that I ask the Tathāgata."
Then, Amoghadarśin spoke these verses:
"How does one practice great wisdom, Extensive wisdom, and swift wisdom?
I now ask this question Of the Great Hero, the Teacher of the World."
How can one attain the profound, subtle, and great wisdom,
the most supreme path to enlightenment?
I pray that the One of Universal Wisdom will explain this.
How does one attain fearlessness and wisdom, skillfully teaching in accordance with others,
and further attain the adamantine mind that gives rise to no delusion regarding the Dharma?
How does one become gentle and supple, with a mind free from all defilement?
The pure precepts are like the ocean—why do they not harbor corpses?
Furthermore, one attains a mind like a mountain—unshakable and inconceivable?
Why does one not place faith in others, nor yet criticize their shortcomings?
Resolutely practicing the wholesome, closing off all evil paths,
abiding in firm resolve, with a joyful and unshakable mind—
how does one give rise to mindfulness?
Abiding here, one is able to see the Buddhas of other lands;
having heard them preach the Dharma, one also encounters the Sangha.
