one sees that odors, tastes, and tangibles are not the Tathāgata, yet that which is distinct from odors, tastes, and tangibles is also not the Tathāgata;
one sees that the mind and mental objects are not the Tathāgata, yet that which is distinct from the mind and mental objects is also not the Tathāgata.
To see that the four great elements are not the Tathāgata, and to see that there is a Tathāgata distinct from the four great elements—
this is likewise true for earth, water, fire, and wind.
When a bodhisattva thus contemplates the continuity of the mind, they attain the wisdom of skillful means regarding all phenomena.
Furthermore, Anagata-darśin!
By what dharma are you able to attain the path to unsurpassed bodhi?
Is it attained by means of the body?
Or is it attained by means of the mind?
If it were attained by means of the body, this body is impure and lacks sentience, being like grass, wood, tiles, or pebbles.
Bodhi is not form; it has no physical substance, its characteristic is empty and quiescent, and it is a dharma that cannot be seen.
Since this body is like grass or wood, devoid of cognition, how can it ever attain the Way of Bodhi?
If one were to attain the unsurpassed path by means of the mind, the mind would have no form or characteristics, being like an illusion or a transformation.
Since bodhi is without mind and likewise without color or appearance—being like an illusion and like a transformation—how could it be attained?
If bodhisattvas attain such an understanding:
that neither the body can attain unsurpassed enlightenment, nor can the mind attain unsurpassed enlightenment, yet unsurpassed enlightenment is attained without being separate from the body and mind.
At that time, the Buddha addressed Akṣayamati, saying:
"One should contemplate the Tathāgata in this manner; he who contemplates in this way is said to have correct contemplation."
Furthermore, Ārya-Amoghadarśin!
When a bodhisattva thus maintains continuous contemplation of phenomena, the mind remains unshakable.
A bodhisattva should understand this deeply; then they shall not regress from the dharma of samādhi.
Furthermore, by always remaining free from a non-continuous mind, one will surely and swiftly attain unsurpassed bodhi.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
“Mind after mind continues in succession, Throughout the past, the future, and the present.”
All you Honored Ones with Universal Eyes, Before long you shall behold the Buddha.
Abiding in the Great Power of the Buddha, Compassionate and bringing benefit to the world,
Mindful of the people in the Land of Men, The Honored One, Sovereign of Virtue.
One should reflect upon past births and deaths, dwelling in the womb, the lineage of one's mother, and the full perfection of physical marks; before long, one shall behold the Buddha.
One should recollect the Buddha’s eighty minor marks as well as the causal conditions of former lives.
Constantly accumulating the most supreme karma, with right mindfulness and a mind intent on wholesome dharmas,
one contemplates the Buddha’s six supernormal powers and his great sovereign penetrations;
thus, precepts, concentration, wisdom, and liberation are all fully accomplished.
How does the supreme teacher attain this ground of tranquility?
By recollecting the World-Honored One who is compassionate toward the world—the most supreme in kindness, joy, and equanimity;
possessed of shame, power, and fearlessness; the teacher of majestic virtue in the world.
Meditating on mindfulness of the Buddha, śamatha, vipaśyanā, and so forth;
furthermore, mindfulness of wisdom and liberation, as well as the three gates of emptiness;
possessing mindfulness and practicing the right efforts, and likewise the bases of psychic power.
Endowed with mindfulness, the faculties, and the powers, as well as the factors of enlightenment,
one who recollects the Buddha transcends birth and cessation, attaining this state of tranquility.
Mindfulness of the inconceivable wholesome dharmas: form and sensation are both pure;
perception, volitional formations, and consciousness are likewise pure.
Meditate on the Buddha’s true golden color, dwelling with a mind free from attachment.
Contemplate what dharma is called "Buddha," maintaining the focus of the mind in constant continuity.
Know that form is not the Tathāgata, and the same applies to the other four aggregates.
The Tathāgata is not apart from the aggregates; one should know this regarding perception and consciousness as well.
One should know that the mind is not the Tathāgata, and the same applies to the dharmas of the ear and so forth;
the Tathāgata is not apart from the eye, and all the dharmas of the five sense-faculties are likewise so.
By contemplating the twelve links of dependent origination, one tames the mind and attains the vision of the Buddha;
by contemplating that the four great elements are not the Buddha, nor is the Buddha something other than these four,
one should understand the twelve links of dependent origination, and seeing the Buddha will not be difficult.
If the aggregates of the Buddhas were the Tathāgata,
then since all sentient beings possess aggregates, they too would be the Tathāgata.
If you wish to attain the faculties and powers, you should contemplate the twelve links of dependent origination.
The aggregates are not the Teacher of the world, nor is there one distinct from the aggregates.
Through the various causes and conditions of the past, they have been continuously and constantly discriminated;
therefore, one is able to grasp the inconceivable power of wisdom.
This body is eternally insentient, like grass, wood, tiles, or pebbles;
bodhi has no form or color, being quiescent and forever unborn.
The body does not touch bodhi, nor does bodhi touch the body.
The mind does not touch awakening, nor does awakening touch the mind;
yet that there can be a characteristic of contact is truly inconceivable.
This is the most supreme state of tranquility of the Buddha, the World-Honored One.
"It is well able to extinguish all the various false views of the non-Buddhists.
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Amoghadarśin addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
“How does a bodhisattva come to know the view of self?
And how, furthermore, should he become free from this view?
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Akṣayamati:

“If a bodhisattva wishes to abandon the view of a self, they must not be attached to any dwelling place; they should rely on the non-reliant. Desiring to benefit all beings with the light of the Dharma;
desiring to blow the Dharma conch and beat the great Dharma drum;
desiring to construct the Dharma ship and establish the Dharma bridge to ferry all sentient beings across the stream of birth and death.”

If one wishes to contemplate the characteristics of the body and its lack of continuity: this body is impure and filled with filth; pus, blood, mucus, and saliva flow constantly from the nine orifices; it is impermanent and subject to decay; it does not abide for even a moment; it is precarious, fragile, and unreliable; it is not to be cherished, being like the false and ignorant speech of an infant.

This body is insubstantial, like a mass of foam upon the water; even if one were to provisionally adorn it with clothing, food and drink, perfumes, and various precious ornaments, indulging it as one pleases for hundreds of thousands of years, it must inevitably perish. It brings no benefit through the long night [of saṃsāra], for such is the nature of this body: it is a phenomenon of birth and death.

Furthermore, they are devoured by insects and beasts; moreover, throughout the long night, they undergo immeasurable suffering in the realms of hell, animals, hungry ghosts, and King Yama, without even a moment's respite.
Furthermore, throughout eternal kalpas within the cycle of birth and death, one serves as a servant for others, driven by them in myriad ways.

This body labors incessantly and undergoes manifold sufferings, yet from the very beginning it is unable to know suffering and sever its habitual tendencies, to realize cessation and cultivate the path, or to practice various meritorious virtues.

Although this body is small, it has received much defilement; one should therefore give this body to all sentient beings—if there are those who cherish their lives, give them life; if they require strength, bestow strength upon them; if they need flesh, give flesh; if they need blood, give blood—one should give to those who have need, but not give what is not requested.

Or, if there is no benefit for that person, he vows to eliminate the delusion of self-view and attain the realization of non-self through the causal conditions of the wholesome mind of relinquishing the body.
While dwelling in this contemplation of relinquishing the body, he no longer clings to the delusion of self-view, cultivating a firm body by means of this non-firm body.
"Furthermore, Aśvaghoṣa!
It is like a village where many children go out together to play by the water's edge.

Seeing a mass of foam on the water, these children compete to seize and toy with it; yet this mass of foam has no self-awareness that it is being toyed with by others, nor does it feel any pain or pleasure."
Thus it is, Aśūnyadarśin!
If there is a bodhisattva who contemplates his own body, he should know that this mind is like that mass of foam, devoid of discrimination.
"If a bodhisattva practices this contemplation, they shall before long attain this profound samādhi, and they shall also swiftly attain unsurpassed bodhi.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"Those who seek the most supreme concentration And wish to attain inconceivable bodhi..."
Forever abandon the view of a self, and always contemplate this body as impermanent,
suffering, and impure— filled with tears, saliva, foul odors, and filth,
with all manner of impurities flowing from its nine orifices; it is truly something to be loathed and dreaded.
Deceptive and devoid of reality, this is a phenomenon subject to decay;
it deludes like a magical illusion and is like a mass of foam upon the water.
This body of mine is fragile and precarious, a dwelling place for sores and ulcers.
Pervaded entirely by foul stench and poison, there is not a single place that can bring joy.
In the beginning, nourishing it brings no benefit; in the end, one becomes food for insects and wolves.
All manner of pleasurable implements and delicacies are provided solely for the sake of this body.
All things must eventually decay and perish; in the end, not a single reality is attained.
Though one exerts oneself for boundless eons, suffering remains constant in its myriad forms;
the realms of hell and animals are the fundamental places where one undergoes torment.
For a long night, hunger and thirst have increased, inconceivable and beyond thought;
oppressed by manifold sufferings, I have thereby strayed from Bodhi.
This body of mine is unreal and should be given as an offering to all sentient beings.
Understanding the Dharma, his heart was free from attachment; whatever was required, he provided it immediately.
Having formed this thought, he then uttered these words:
"I now relinquish this body; take its blood and flesh as you please."
"If there be those who cherish their lives, I shall bestow longevity upon them.
Sacrificing his own body to save sentient beings, he attained samādhi through his illness.
Seeking water-foam piece by piece, he never found anything solid or substantial.
"My own body is also like this; though one seeks the truth, it cannot be found.
If one attains this right contemplation, one will swiftly accomplish the path to Bodhi.
At that time, the World-Honored One smiled.
The Dharma of all Buddhas, Tathāgatas, is always thus:

when the World-Honored One smiles, various colored rays of light—blue, yellow, red, white, crimson, green, and crystal-like—issue forth from his face, ascending as far as the Brahma Heaven. From there they return downward, circling the Buddha three times before re-entering the crown of his head.
That light suddenly vanished in an instant.
The Elder Ānanda immediately rose from his seat, adjusted his robes, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and asked in verse:
"O Most Victorious One, Honored Tamer, A smile is never without cause."
O Unsurpassed Teacher of the World, I pray that you will explain for me:
by what causes and conditions do you manifest this smile?
O One adorned with a hundred merits and golden hue, you who are well-versed in the ultimate truth.
One who pities and benefits others is the refuge for the world.
For what cause and condition do you manifest this smile?
You are the peerless Honored One among men, the supreme one beyond compare.
The Tathāgata’s myriad virtues are pure, wondrous, and free from blemish.
For what cause and condition do you manifest this smile?
O World-Honored One who abides in sublime great compassion, the one to whom all turn for refuge—
Having already abandoned all afflictions, with a pure and disciplined voice,
I pray that you will explain for me the cause and condition of your smile.
Who today is worthy to receive such profound and vast meaning?
Who dwells upon the firm ground?
Which land has encountered auspiciousness?
O Honored One to whom the world turns for refuge, for what reason do you manifest a smile?
O Tamer of Men, who is the refuge for all; pray tell me.
I wish to hear the cause and condition for the smile of the Pure One.
If the Noble One would deign to explain it, my doubts will be forever removed.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Ānanda, saying:
"When I previously spoke of this contemplation of continuity, thirty thousand people attained the pure Dharma-eye;
eighty quadrillion nayutas of devas likewise became free from defilement, and their Dharma-eyes were purified."
Furthermore, thirty trillion nayutas of bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs realized the stage of Anāgāmin;
additionally, thirty thousand bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās attained the patience of non-arising (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti);

and thirty thousand sentient beings gave rise to the bodhicitta, immediately beginning to cultivate the practices of a bodhisattva, destined to all attain Buddhahood during the Bhadra Kalpa—this was their first generation of the mind for the unsurpassed path.

Furthermore, there were ninety trillion nayutas of sentient beings who all attained non-retrogression from the path to Bodhi; they shall become Buddhas named Fangguang (Radiant Light), Ligouzun (Stainless Honored One), Śākyamuni, Rìguāngxiàng (Sun-Phase) Buddha, Yuèguāngmíng (Moon-Luminosity) Buddha, and Tiánzhōngzūn (Honored One Among Gods).
Additionally, ninety-two billion nayutas of beings resolved their minds toward the state of a śrāvaka and shall become arhats.
At that time, when the World-Honored One spoke these words, his voice shook the trichiliocosm.

With his divine eye, the Buddha beheld ninety billion hundred thousand nayutas of Buddha-fields in the ten directions; within them, all sentient beings saw the Tathāgata emitting a ray of light from between his brows called "Blazing Radiance," which illuminated the ten directions everywhere.
When sentient beings saw this, their hearts were struck with awe and their hair stood on end.

At that time, among the immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of nayutas of sentient beings in that land who encountered this light, some attained the fruit of *srotāpanna*, *sakṛdāgāmin*, *anāgāmin*, and *arhat*.

Many sentient beings gave rise to the bodhicitta and all became non-retrogressive regarding unsurpassed enlightenment; they shall become Buddhas in future ages, all bearing the same name—Avaivartika (Non-retrogressive).
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to proclaim and illuminate this meaning clearly, spoke again in verse:
"When I previously proclaimed this, observing the continuity of the mind,
there were sixty thousand and ninety-nine billion beings."
Because of the benefit of hearing the Dharma, they have resolved their minds upon Bodhi;
furthermore, thirty thousand people have all attained the noble eye of wisdom,
having heard and continuously reflected upon the Bodhi of tranquil concentration.
All these shall be entirely freed from the hardships and sufferings of the evil realms;
eighty trillion devas, having heard the voice of the Tathāgata,
have attained the pure Dharma-eye and shall forever be parted from the suffering of the miserable destinies.
Thirty trillion members of the fourfold assembly attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas;
they were delivered from all evil realms and were no longer subject to the afflictions of suffering.
They shall surely attain the Way of the Buddha, like the flourishing blossoms of spring.
Thirty trillion people, training in the path to enlightenment,
shall likewise attain the great majestic power of all Buddhas;
having realized the unsurpassed way, they will show compassion for the world.
Sixty thousand sons of gods, training for awakening,
practice the conduct that is the joy among joys, just like the Honored Maitreya.
The unimpeded refuge of the world brings vast benefit through his smile.
“Ānanda!
You should know that because all things have causes and conditions, it is for this reason that I today manifest this smile.
Chapter Eleven: The Chapter on King Subtle-Secret (*Sūkṣma-rahasya-rāja-varga*). At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Amoghadarśin addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

How should a bodhisattva-mahāsattva know how to dwell securely in such dharmas as shame (*hrī*), remorse (*apatrāpya*), and dread (*bhaya*), so as to abandon the lack of shame and remorse and attain this samādhi?”
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Akṣayamati:

"It is for this reason that these bodhisattvas feel shame and remorse; they harbor shame and fear when they commit various evils with their bodies, and they give rise to disgrace when they perform evil deeds with their speech and minds. It is the same regarding envy and indolence."

If one gives rise to unwholesome [thoughts] yet feels reverence for the Buddhas and fear of the devas and worldly people because evil and unwholesome dharmas are shameful, then the bodhisattva thus abides in shame and dread.

Abandoning shamelessness, fearlessness, and all unwholesome dharmas, diligently cultivating various virtues and guarding pure conduct, remaining silent and secluded, and perfecting the three karmas, you shall before long also attain this samādhi. In birth after birth, you will always encounter the Buddhas and shall swiftly attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
"Furthermore, Aśvaghoṣa!
How marvelous, how rare!

I recall that in the past, throughout incalculable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of nayutas of kalpas, there was first a third kalpa named Sujāta, followed by a kalpa named Ratnolkā, and subsequently a kalpa named Padmahrada."
When the turbid kalpa had arisen and one thousand years remained, there followed another kalpa named "Abiding in Bliss.
At that time, a king was born within this kalpa named Jyotismat (Victorious Subtlety); he possessed great majesty and power, and his dominion was sovereign.

The city where the king resided was named Kusuma-vimala-gandha-rāśi; it was seventy yojanas in length and breadth, adorned with twelve tiers of the seven precious jewels, and its magnificent splendor was like that of the city of Supratiṣṭhita.
To the north of the city there is a place called Vimalā.

There is a grove in this location named Kṣema, which is perfectly square, measuring ten yojanas on each side. It is surrounded on all sides by many tala trees; the layout of this grove is like that of the well-constructed garden.
Furthermore, Āśvaghoṣa!

At that time, there was a Buddha named Vairocana (Luminous Appearance) Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidhyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān, who appeared in the world.
The Buddha told Akṣayamati:

"At that time, the Buddha Prabhāsa resided with his retinue in the Anavya Garden. He was accompanied by nine hundred and ninety billion nayutas of bhikṣus, all of whom were arhats whose outflows were exhausted, who were free from further afflictions, who had attained mastery over their minds, who had accomplished what was to be done, and who had fully mastered everything that ought to be learned."
The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Prabhāsvara, having dressed in his robes and taken up his alms bowl at dawn, entered the city for alms accompanied by a retinue of bhikṣus.

At that time, King Sūkṣma, hearing that the Buddha was coming, mounted his great elephant named Māgadha and, preceded and followed by countless hundreds of thousands of attendants, went out from the city together to welcome the World-Honored One.
"Furthermore, Aśvaghoṣa!
When King Sūkṣma-darśana saw from afar the Buddha approaching, with his radiant complexion and marks of excellence so subtle, wondrous, and extraordinary, he was filled with great joy."

Having dismounted from his elephant, he approached the Tathāgata, prostrated with his head at the Buddha's feet, and circumambulated him three times to the right; he then requested the Buddha and the Saṃgha along the road.
At that time, the Buddha Mingxiang (Prabhūtaratna) silently granted his consent.

Once the King knew that the Buddha had accepted his invitation, he immediately swept and sprinkled the ground that very night, burned incense, and prepared various kinds of rare and exquisite offerings.

Furthermore, he erected banners and streamers throughout the city, hung flower garlands, necklaces, and precious canopies, and sprinkled the dust with ox-head sandalwood juice. He scattered various flowers to adorn the ground and placed caskets filled with flowers before the seat, performing many kinds of wonderful music as an offering.
"Furthermore, Aśvaghoṣa!
Having prepared the offerings, at the time of dawn, the king, together with his retinue, went to the An-yin Garden (Anavaśānta-udyāna) to pay homage to the Tathāgata and addressed him, saying:
'World-Honored One!'"
"The time for the meal has arrived.

When the Buddha Prabhāsa heard the King's invitation, he immediately manifested great supernormal powers according to those signs; together with the bhikṣus, he ascended into the void and emitted ninety-one million pure rays of light that illuminated the eastern direction;
the same occurred in the other three directions.

Within each ray of light are eighty billion nayutas of various exquisite lotuses; upon each lotus is a manifested Tathāgata, complete with all the marks and signs of perfection, just like the Buddha Prabhūtaratna.
These Tathāgatas have immeasurable retinues; with Śakra attending on their left and Brahmā attending on their right, they are no different from the true Śakras and Brahmās.
"Furthermore, Aśvaghoṣa!

When the Tathāgata Prabhāsa manifested these various signs of supernatural transformation, in a single moment of thought, the gods of the desire and form realms produced immeasurable varieties of exquisite music and offered worship to the Tathāgata Prabhāsa with celestial sandalwood, *tāmālapatra*, aloeswood, flower garlands, and other such fragrances."
Then that World-Honored One preached the Dharma for the king, saying:

"Great King, you should know that all conditioned phenomena are impermanent; all that is formed is suffering; because they lack reality, they are empty; and in all dharmas, there is no self whatsoever."
Why is this so? This body is impure; its nine orifices flow with filth like worms in excrement. It is subject to decay and is fragile, not remaining still for even a single thought-moment.
The four elements and the various aggregates are provisionally combined to form this body, which is constantly assailed by hunger, thirst, cold, and heat.

Deceptive, illusory, and like a mirage or a mass of foam upon water, these phenomena lack self-mastery and are subject to decay; yet they are forcibly designated as "persons," though not a single one can be relied upon.

Therefore, Great King, you should observe deeply that all conditioned phenomena of birth and death are utterly loathsome; you should diligently apply skillful means to seek swift liberation from them.
At that time, having heard these words, King Sūkṣma joined his palms toward the Buddha and spoke thus:
“So it is, World-Honored One!
It is truly as the Holy Teaching declares.”
Conditioned phenomena are impermanent, suffering, and empty; all dharmas are entirely without self.
One clearly perceives that this body is impure and foul-smelling, a mass of manifold sufferings, and truly loathsome.
At that time, having witnessed the Buddha’s miraculous manifestations and having heard the Dharma taught by the Tathāgata, the king immediately resolved to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
"Furthermore, Aśvaghoṣa!

At that time, the Tathāgata, knowing that the king had already resolved his mind upon Bodhi, accepted the king's invitation together with the great assembly; they traveled through the air and descended once they reached the city."
The king followed the Buddha on foot to the palace gate; having offered a seat, they sat down in order.

The king, together with his ministers, the female members of the inner court, and the people of the realm, stood in attendance at his left and right. Holding up various offerings, they received the Buddha’s blessings and vows, and each was given food until they were fully satisfied.
When the meal was finished, they rinsed their mouths and washed their hands, and further made offerings with various flowers, incense, music, exquisite garments, and superior jewels.

At that time, on that very day, King Sūkṣma-rāja renounced the four continents as well as eighty-four billion nayutas of queens, consorts, and maidservants; he entrusted the royal throne to his eldest son and, together with eighty billion nayutas of people, went to the presence of the Tathāgata Prabhūta-pradīpa to leave the household life and practice the Way.
After the King had renounced the household life and was about to request the Dharma, he addressed [the Buddha], saying:
"World-Honored One!
How does a bodhisattva attain the buddha-remembrance samādhi (*buddhānusmṛti-samādhi*) taught by all the Buddhas?"
"If a person can attain this samādhi, they shall swiftly realize anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi and fully perceive the Dharma.
At that time, the Buddha Prabhāsa said to the bhikṣu Guhyaka:
"A bodhisattva has two dharmas by which they attain this samādhi and shall likewise swiftly realize unsurpassed bodhi."
What are these two dharmas?
A bodhisattva should have faith in the sūtras spoken by the Tathāgata, which are this Great Vaipulya, the sphere of practice of all Buddhas.
A bodhisattva who is fully endowed with these two dharmas attains this samādhi and shall swiftly attain Buddhahood.
Furthermore, there are two dharmas.
What are these two? They are śamatha and vipaśyanā.
Furthermore, they possess two dharmas:
relinquishing both self and non-self, and abiding securely in the dharmas of shame, remorse, and dread.
If a bodhisattva can possess these two dharmas, they will attain this samādhi and swiftly achieve perfect enlightenment.
He addressed Akṣayamati:
"The bhikṣu Sūkṣma said to the Buddha Prabhāsa:
'How does a bodhisattva, by abiding in the dharmas of shame, remorse, and dread, attain this samādhi?'"
The Tathāgata Mingxiang addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
"A bodhisattva should abandon the three evil karmas, shamelessness, lack of remorse, and all other unwholesome dharmas, and abide in the dharmas of shame, remorse, and dread."

Furthermore, this bodhisattva, being fully endowed with a sense of shame and dread of wrongdoing, abandons all unwholesome states and practices wholesome dharmas; he should guard his pure actions of body, speech, and mind.
"Furthermore, Aśvaghoṣa!

At that time, having heard the discourse on the faults of transgression from that Buddha, the bhikṣu immediately abandoned shamelessness and the fear of all evils; he applied himself with diligence to collecting his mind, abided in all wholesome dharmas, did not lose those wholesome dharmas, and desired to bring them to fulfillment."

Furthermore, he again collects his mind and dwells in right contemplation—contemplating that all phenomena neither increase nor decrease, and perceiving no coming or going, nor arising or ceasing, among phenomena.
"When the Bhikṣu Sūkṣma-mati contemplates in this way, he does not perceive any phenomena as having various characteristics.
He contemplates the twelve links of dependent origination as being like a dream or a mirage;
he contemplates all phenomena as being like shadows, illusions, and transformations."
Contemplating all phenomena, there is neither increase nor decrease;
contemplating all phenomena, they have no name and no intrinsic nature;
contemplating all phenomena, there is neither cessation nor arising.
If the Bodhisattva Subtle and Secret practices in this manner, he shall before long attain this samādhi.
Having attained this samādhi, his eloquence will be uninterrupted, and after sixty trillion nayutas of kalpas, he shall attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
The Buddha told Akṣayamati:
"Do not give rise to doubt. Was the King Sūkṣma, who at that time renounced his kingdom to leave the household life and study the Path, anyone other than this?"
This is the Tathāgata Padmottara Buddha.
The Bodhisattva Sūkṣmadhātu dwells in shame and modesty, cultivates and accomplishes all wholesome dharmas, and before long attains such a samādhi as this.
"Furthermore, Aśvaghoṣa!

I now tell you that regarding this Buddha-remembrance samādhi (buddhānusmṛti-samādhi) taught by all Buddhas, if there are sentient beings who have not planted roots of goodness, they shall never hear of such a samādhi."
He addressed Akṣayamati:

"If sons or daughters of good family have, in the past, drawn near to, made offerings to, and planted many roots of merit before immeasurable Buddhas, only then shall they be able to hear this King of Samādhis, a jewel."
How much more so for those who copy, read, recite, receive and uphold, analyze and explain, and contemplate the meaning and intent [of this sutra]?
These sons and daughters of good family will plant roots of goodness that are immeasurable, boundless, and beyond calculation.
These individuals, who practice the Bodhisattva vehicle, shall now hear this samādhi for the first time and will, in due course, attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi;
with the sole exception of those who have already realized it through bodily witness.

If a bodhisattva cultivates this samādhi, they will always be born in the Pure Lands and never be separated from seeing the Buddhas; they will possess all mundane and supramundane eloquence and shall certainly and swiftly attain unsurpassed bodhi.”
At that time, the king suddenly awoke from his dream in a startle; yet he still saw this deva standing right before him. He then addressed the deva, saying:
"Who is able to receive and uphold such a profound samādhi of mindfulness of the Buddha?"
The deity said to the king:
"Not far from here there is a great bhikṣu named Śālavatī, who constantly delights in receiving, upholding, reciting, expounding, and practicing according to the teachings this profound samādhi."
At that time, Śakraketu received this samādhi and the name of the bhikṣu from that deva; he remembered and upheld them with a sincere mind, never allowing them to be forgotten.

Then, at the break of dawn, he renounced the four continents, the golden wheel, the seven treasures, and eighty trillion countless hundreds of thousands of palace ladies and court beauties; for the sake of seeking the profound Dharma of samādhi, he immediately left the household life together with his retinue and went as one to the bhikṣu Śālavṛkṣarāja.
"Furthermore, Aśvaghoṣa!

At that time, those four assemblies and the eight classes of beings, including devas and nāgas, all surrounded him together. There were ninety trillion devas of the desire realm and eighty thousand nayutas of bodhisattvas, who also respectfully surrounded him with their retinues."
At that time, while the Bhikṣu Śālavatī was preaching this profound *buddhānusmṛti-samādhi* to the great assembly,
King Indradhvaja went to his presence, scattered celestial jewels over the Bhikṣu, and prostrated himself with his five limbs touching the ground in wholehearted veneration.
Furthermore, he took eighty thousand pure and exquisite golden flowers, celestial *mandārava* blossoms, and powdered aloeswood incense, and with a heart of reverence, scattered them over the bhikṣu.
Having completed these offerings, he and his entire retinue immediately went forth from the household life and donned the pure dharma robes.
Desiring to cultivate this samādhi, he made offerings to immeasurable Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, together with their retinues, seeking this very samādhi.

For eighty-four thousand *koṭi-nayuta* years, he attended upon and made offerings of robes, food and drink, and various precious jewels to the Bhikṣu King of Trees. He himself constantly upheld, recited, explained, and practiced according to the teachings this wondrous samādhi; furthermore, with great compassion as his heart, he transformed all immeasurable sentient beings without ever succumbing to weariness or indolence.

When the Bodhisattva Imperial Banner and his retinue heard this sublime Dharma taught by the Teacher King of Trees, they received and upheld it with a sincere heart, never abandoning it for even a moment. They gave rise to profound reverence, always regarding him as the Buddha, and practiced with diligent application, never resting.

The Bhikṣu Śālavṛkṣarāja fully brought all those eighty trillion hundred thousand bhikṣus to accomplishment; they cultivated the bodhisattva practice and dwelt in the stage of non-retrogression, after which he entered parinirvāṇa.
All those attendants also passed away.
At that time, there appeared another Buddha in the world, named the Tathāgata, World-Honored One Jambudhvaja, fully endowed with the ten titles.

Having encountered the World-Honored One, the bhikṣu Di-chuang made offerings and paid him respect; he inquired about and received instruction on this profound samādhi, upholding, reciting, and practicing it according to the teaching. He benefited all beings in the world of humans and devas, enabling them all to attain the great benefit of unsurpassed bodhi.

Because the bhikṣu Di-tiāng (Imperial Banner) has extensively proclaimed and disseminated the profound samādhis taught by all Buddhas, he shall attain perfect enlightenment after three thousand kalpas; furthermore, he will bring to fulfillment a retinue of immeasurable hundreds of thousands of nayutas—nine billion in number—all of whom shall dwell securely in non-retrogressive bodhi.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Akṣayamati:
"Was the great bhikṣu King Indradhvaja someone else?
He is none other than the one who has now attained Buddhahood, known as the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, and Perfectly Enlightened One named Uccagāmin, fully endowed with the ten titles."
"Furthermore, Aśvaghoṣa!

You should now know that by the majestic power and spiritual authority of this samādhi, you have benefited such immeasurable sentient beings; because of having heard even a little [of this teaching], you shall always encounter the era of a Buddha."
Furthermore, Amoghadarśin! If there are bodhisattvas who,
by merely hearing the name of this samādhi even once, will always encounter the era of a Buddha—
how much more so for those bodhisattvas who, in the present, hear and encounter this sūtra of the samādhi, and receive, uphold, read, and recite it?

The merit of this is already immeasurable as described above; how much more so for one who can further hear it extensively, receive and uphold it, read and recite it, explain it, and practice according to its teaching?
"Furthermore, Anaviladarśana!
Whether there be bodhisattvas who have mounted the Great Vehicle, the Pratyekabuddha Vehicle, the Śrāvaka Vehicle,

or the vehicles of humans and devas— if good sons and good daughters, or others, should even briefly hear this wondrous samādhi, all these bodhisattvas and good sons and daughters shall swiftly attain unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment.
Furthermore, Ārya-avalokita!

These people are like someone in Jambudvīpa who, seeing the signs of dawn, knows with certainty that the sun will rise before long and its great light will shine everywhere; by means of the sun’s radiance, the people of Jambudvīpa are able to distinguish colors such as blue, yellow, and so forth.
Thus it is, Aśūnyadarśin!

If there are practitioners who hear even briefly of the samādhis taught by the Buddhas, these sons and daughters of good family will before long attain unsurpassed bodhi, just as one recognizes from the appearance of light that the sun will surely rise.
"You should have deep faith in this wondrous samādhi; receive, uphold, and keep it in mind, and do not give rise to doubt or confusion.
Furthermore, Anagata-darśin!
Just as when a kalpa is nearing its end and six suns appear, the entire great earth becomes smoke and flame; [so too shall it be for those who practice this samādhi]."
When seven suns arise, the entire trichiliocosm will blaze forth with light.
In this same way, Akṣayamati!

Whether they are sons or daughters of good family who study the Mahāyāna or those who do not, if they hear even a little of this jewel-like samādhi—whether by writing it down, upholding it, reading and reciting it, or explaining its meaning—they shall all swiftly attain unsurpassed bodhi.
Furthermore, Āśūnyapratihata!
Good sons and others, it is like digging a well: if one sees mud, one certainly knows that water is not far off.
"Furthermore, Āśūnyapratihata!"

If there are bodhisattvas or any sentient beings who, regarding the Buddha’s teaching on the *buddhānusmṛti-samādhi*, should write it down, receive and uphold it, read and recite it, explain its meaning, practice according to the teaching, and remember it without forgetting, these sons and daughters of good family will before long swiftly attain unsurpassed bodhi.
"Furthermore, Aśvaghoṣa!

Good sons, it is as if there were a person who swallowed a vajra pill; at that time, wise good sons would certainly know that this person will surely die before long, because this vajra is extremely difficult to digest."
Thus it is, Aśūnyapratibhāna!

If sons of good family uphold, recite, and extensively explain the profound meaning of this wondrous treasure of samādhi, or even hear as little as this sublime dharma of samādhi, these sons and daughters of good family shall before long attain unsurpassed bodhi.

Why is this? Because the Buddha-remembrance samādhi (*buddhānusmṛti-samādhi*) taught by all Buddhas is like a vajra; it has been proclaimed, analyzed, and discerned by the Buddhas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas of the past, future, and present, and is protected by their majestic spiritual power, so that practitioners do not lose their practice.
A bodhisattva should practice in this manner, constantly desiring to benefit all the world; this is called the bodhisattva’s vehicle of joyful practice.
It is like the Garden of Joy in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, where anyone who beholds it experiences exuberant delight in body and mind.

When a bodhisattva thus attains this samādhi, they will swiftly achieve unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment; furthermore, regarding those chapters and phrases they have not yet heard, if they wish to study them, it will not be difficult for them to attain mastery.
How wonderful!

In the past, all Buddhas, for the sake of benefiting others, manifested various teachings through analytical exposition, fulfilling the meaning of the words and causing them to abide securely within the Dharma-realm.
The great Bodhisattvas upheld and protected these teachings, expounding and transforming beings to lead them to delight in the Right Path.
“Such is the sequence of the ritual for this Dharma-gate; all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should know it.
Furthermore, Anagata-darśin!
If there are bodhisattvas who hear even a small portion of this samādhi spoken by these Buddhas, all such persons shall swiftly attain unsurpassed bodhi.”
Furthermore, Amoghadarśin!
For this reason, I shall now analyze, reveal, and expound it for you.

You should also know that if one hears this Buddha-remembrance samādhi (buddhānusmṛti-samādhi) spoken by all the Buddhas, and receives, upholds, and explains it, one will before long swiftly attain the path of unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment (anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi).

Therefore, you should now receive, uphold, read, recite, and practice it, even to the point of copying it; furthermore, you should extensively explain and analyze it for all fourfold assemblies, as well as for kings, ministers, śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, and followers of other teachings.
Why is this? If these beings hear [this teaching], they shall attain the fulfillment of unsurpassed bodhi.
Furthermore, Anagata-darśin!
If good sons or good daughters should, with resolute sincerity and pure faith, embrace this profound samādhi. Why is this?
Because it has been praised by all the Buddhas of the past.

You should now, with an inconceivable mind and a sincere heart, remember and uphold this; believe deeply in this samādhi and practice it with diligent effort, so that the continuity of the mind is maintained. Why is this?
This samādhi consists entirely of the true teachings of all Buddhas.

"Furthermore, Aśvaghoṣa!

Why is this? Because the profound and sublime scripture on the Buddha-remembrance samādhi (buddhānusmṛti-samādhi) taught by all Buddhas is able to bestow upon sentient beings unfailing fruits, and it also enables the practitioner to attain boundless merit.
"If there are those who hear this, such persons shall obtain an inconceivable mass of immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) merits.
Furthermore, *Aśūnyapratikṣaṇa*!"

Akṣayamati replied:

World-Honored One!

This samādhi spoken of by the Buddhas is the foremost reality, uttered from the very mouth of the Buddha; if one can write it down, receive and uphold it, read and recite it, expound it, and analyze and explain it, it will produce an immeasurable mass of merit, the blessing of which far exceeds the former merit."
How much more so for those who, having heard it, encourage others to receive and uphold it, and extensively analyze and explain it for the fourfold assembly?
Furthermore, Anagamin!
I now declare that this accumulation of the jewels of merit is inexhaustible.

Abiding in those various worlds, amidst the presence of many who possess worldly wisdom,

if you seek to study the Buddha’s wisdom, you shall become equal to the Tathāgata.

If one seeks the bodhi of the Buddha, one will then obtain the power of great fruition.
Majestic and most exquisite, his form and appearance are like pure gold.

he is fully endowed with inconceivable and all-encompassing virtues.
Pure form adorned by a hundred merits, the supreme jewel of the world,
incomparable honor among gods and humans— neither dragons nor ghosts can fathom him. Relying upon Bodhi,

"For the sake of benefiting sentient beings, He reveals the Dharma of profound meditative concentration. Chapter Fifteen:

Right Mindfulness The Bodhisattva Sutra on the Samādhi of Recollecting the Buddha, Chapter Fifteen: Right Mindfulness At that time, within the assembly, the Bodhisattvas Siyi (Contemplating Meaning), She feiyi (Abandoning What Is Not Meaning), Xinyongjian (Courageous and Strong in Mind), Fenbiexin (Discerning Mind), Wuqianyi (Non-avaricious Mind), Babanrao (Uprooting Afflictions), Sansiyi (Skillfully Contemplating Meaning), Zhongzhi (Multitudinous Wisdom), Wubuo (Unbound), Zhongguang (Multitudinous Light), Zhidengguang (Light of Wisdom), Zaoshi zhishi (Creating Wisdom as an Object of Knowledge), and Wudeng fan'ao (Incomparable Afflictions), along with the Devaputras Di-chuang and Tiaohua, all together paid respectful homage and addressed the World-Honored One:
"Now, regarding what is called 'that which has been spoken by all Buddhas,' for what reason is it named 'that which has been spoken by all Buddhas'?"
What are the Buddhas?
What constitutes a Buddha?
How should one practice mindfulness so that it is called "recollection of the Buddha"?
"Do you give rise to mindfulness of the body,
or do you give rise to mindfulness of phenomena?
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bodhisattvas:
“Excellent, excellent, sons of good family!

What you have asked is profound and inconceivable; it is entirely through the power of the Buddha’s majestic spiritual authority that you have given rise to this unhindered eloquence of joyful exposition.”
That which is spoken by all Buddhas is called the Buddha’s teaching.
To maintain right mindfulness of the true characteristics of all phenomena is called mindfulness of the Buddha.
What is meant by right mindfulness?

Do not cling to any evils or slanders; you should cultivate all dharmas that are beyond reproach. You should remain detached from both "self" and "non-self," and not perceive sentient beings, a life-span, a soul, a nourisher, a person, a human, or a being. Do not cling to an agent, one who causes another to act, the aggregates (*skandhas*), the elements (*dhātus*), the sense-bases (*āyatanas*), or the objects of perception.

Regarding all dharmas—from this life and future lives up to the three realms—there is no reliance and no defiled view of self; there is neither grasping nor abandoning toward any conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*). There are immeasurable wholesome dharmas, such as meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), liberation (*vimokṣa*), the six supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), the bases of power (*ṛddhipāda*), the faculties (*indriya*), the powers (*bala*), the factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*), and the great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*); briefly stated, these include ninety trillion *nayuta* inconceivable and profound samādhis.

The Dharma constantly contemplated by all Buddhas—the Buddha’s wisdom of skillful means—those who accordingly transcribe, recite, and expound the Vaipulya sutras and proclaim the merits of the Buddha are said to be "speaking what the Buddha has spoken."
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
“Always able to relinquish all conditioned things, which are characterized by emptiness and instability;
Not grasping at the intrinsic nature of any phenomena— Then one attains this samādhi.”
Do not cling to various slanders, nor to recollections and conceptual discriminations;
forever free from "self" and "what belongs to self," one thus attains samādhi.
Do not perceive sentient beings, a life-span, or a person within the phenomena of the aggregates.
The self, the person, the agent, the individual, the nourisher, and so forth—
when there is no conceptualization regarding these, this is called "teaching the Dharma."
Untainted by any phenomena, Regarding self-nature and what belongs to self,
Seeing that the "I" is not born from the aggregates— Then one attains this samādhi.
Form, sensation, perception, formations, and consciousness— All are empty and signless.
The root is fundamentally impure; by knowing this, one attains samādhi.
Contemplating all conditioned phenomena, one sees they arise from conditions and lack autonomy;
all are unreal, deceptive, and ungraspable.
Just as those phenomena arise from conditions, so too is this called the eye-base;
the ear, nose, and others are likewise all devoid of intrinsic nature.
If one can discern them with true insight, one will attain this samādhi.
This body is empty and lacks reality; this collection of aggregates contains not a single purity.
Nine orifices flow with pus and blood—who could find delight in such a place?
The mind enters and perishes moment by moment; it is illusory and ever like a phantom.
If one can discern deeply, one will attain this samādhi.
All the sense-bases (*āyatana*) and so forth are entirely empty and lack reality;
ordinary beings are like small children, deludedly conceiving of a self.
Deluded by craving, one does not know this is illusory;
this body is like an empty village, a dwelling place for many thieves.
This deceptive dharma is a source of affliction; the wise always feel weary of it and seek detachment.
By observing thus in depth, one attains this samādhi.
The aggregates, elements, and sense bases—all phenomena—are empty; not a single one is real.
If a person can discern this, they shall give birth to this samādhi.
Like a flame, a bubble, a mass of foam, An illusion, a transformation, or a plantain tree—
One should contemplate the body as precarious and fragile, Even more unreal than these.
If these bodhisattvas do not disparage such wisdom,
they will swiftly attain the profound samādhi taught by all Buddhas.
All phenomena are not self-born, nor do they arise from another.
Ultimately there is no abiding; the untainted dharmas are likewise so.
If one can contemplate in this way, then this samādhi will arise.
One abandons all conditioned things and the characteristics of the transformation of all formations.
This Dharma is like space; no arising can be found therein.
When a bodhisattva understands this and trains in all dharmas, they swiftly attain supreme enlightenment and turn the unsurpassed wheel of Dharma.
This bodhisattva is then able to establish the banner of the Dharma;
with inconceivable wisdom, they discern all phenomena,
seeing them all as deceptive and ultimately unreal.
"Although I have now proclaimed this samādhi to you and its ritual characteristics,
its meaning is exceedingly difficult to understand.
At that time, when the World-Honored One spoke this Dharma, there were bodhisattvas who attained the patience of non-arising (anutpattika-dharmakṣānti) and further dwelt in the buddhānusmṛti-samādhi.

All these bodhisattvas saw, in the eastern direction, as many Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, as there are grains of sand in the Ganges, all preaching this samādhi—pure and equal, without increase and without decrease, non-dual and without distinction.

It was likewise in all other directions; in each, there were immeasurable billions of nayutas of Tathāgatas, World-Honored Ones, who simultaneously expounded the Buddha-remembrance samādhi taught by all Buddhas.

At that time, when the bodhisattvas heard what the Buddha had spoken, their bodies and minds were filled with joy; they attained a sense of sublime peace and happiness, and could not contain their exultation. They then spoke of his appearance before the Buddha once more in verse:
"We take refuge in the Light of the World, The Perfectly Awakened One, the Honored Muni."
The Great Dharma’s Holy King of Physicians, Śākyamuni Buddha, ocean of wisdom, Is the Lion King upon whom humanity relies; he universally displays all forms and marks.
Beholding those lands in the eastern direction, there are nayutas of Buddhas.
Out of compassion for sentient beings, he preaches the Dharma like a lion.
He tames *nayutas* of such bodhisattvas as these,
who dwell in the stage of youthful innocence and have attained the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
Skillfully conforming to the profound nature, they do not destroy the Dharma.
In the other nine directions, the signs are likewise;
they see many billions of beings and nayutas of Buddhas.
Like the lion king, the refuge of those who fear,
Untainted, tranquil, and peerless, he turns the supreme wheel of Dharma.
In this place there is no coming or going, And its characteristic likewise does not abide.
All phenomena lack reality; their nature is empty, without arising or ceasing.
Sentient beings, life-span, and the person are likewise so;
all aggregates, elements, and sense-bases lack reality, like an empty fist.
Just as wild beasts have ultimately no place of reliance, so too all phenomena are truly without arising. Some are eternally impure;
with defiled minds, they crave birth and death like foolish infants.
For many billions of nayutas of kalpas, they have constantly endured suffering without weariness;
therefore, out of compassion, the Buddha has taught this Bodhi for their sake.
For this reason, O sons of the Buddhas, you should always sacrifice your bodies, hands, and feet.
One's head, eyes, marrow, and brain, one's wife, children, and exquisite treasures—all these can be relinquished;
by means of this, one practices for bodhi.
Having been able to give away one's wife and children, as well as kinsmen and all external wealth,
and furthermore having renounced celestial and worldly status, as well as one’s own body, flesh, sinews, and bones—
one who can relinquish such things that are difficult to relinquish will swiftly attain perfect enlightenment.
Giving and ethical discipline yield the most excellent fruits; likewise patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom.
By practicing loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity, one seeks unsurpassed knowledge.
“A Bodhisattva should cultivate this for the sake of benefiting sentient beings.
At that time, the World-Honored One replied to the bodhisattvas in verse:
“If a bodhisattva, throughout many eons, practices according to suchness...”
Neither different nor discriminated—by this is bodhi explained.
Its nature is profoundly quiescent; it is difficult to attain and difficult to see.
"One should arouse an inexhaustible intention and cultivate such practices;
thus the bodhisattva will attain progress in wisdom and draw near to enlightenment.
At that time, the World-Honored One briefly explained four dharmas for the sake of the bodhisattvas—in order to fulfill their enlightenment—and addressed them, saying:
"O sons of good family!
You should study the precepts, guarding and observing them with diligent self-restraint;
you should give rise to the skillful means of wisdom and constantly practice them with perseverance until you reach enlightenment."
One should constantly give rise to a mind of loving-kindness toward all sentient beings;
in order to eliminate the view of self and the notion of "mine," one seeks the most supreme, unsurpassed bodhi.
To that end, even at the cost of sacrificing one's body, life, and wealth, one should protect, accomplish, and increase [this resolve].
"These four dharmas are the root of samādhi. Chapter Sixteen:

The Great Assembly Upholds [the Teaching] At that time, the World-Honored One knew that the great assembly of ninety trillion nayutas of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas had all gathered, as well as hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of bodhisattvas who were destined to abide in the stage of non-retrogression during the time of Maitreya Buddha.
At that time, there were ninety-nine billion, one hundred thousand nayutas of bodhisattvas in the eastern direction, with the Bodhisattva Brahmottara as their leader;
in the southern direction, there were likewise ninety-nine billion bodhisattvas, with the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Satyadhara and others as their leaders;
and in the western direction, there were ninety-nine thousand bodhisattvas, with the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Mahāprajña and others as their leaders.
Furthermore, from the north, there were ninety-nine thousand bodhisattvas, with the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Great Light (Mahāprabha) as their leader.
Additionally, immeasurable bodhisattvas dwelling in that world of Tuṣita all came to assemble, as did the Brahmakāyika deva kings, the Great Flower Brahmā King, and immeasurable other Brahmā Kings.
Furthermore, there were boundless hundreds of thousands of nayutas of Śakras, the Indras of the Gods, with Saṃjñeya, the Lord of the Gods, as their chief.
There were also immeasurable hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of the Four Great Heavenly Kings. Furthermore, there were immeasurable Kāla yakṣas, Mālādhara yakṣas, and Sadāmada yakṣas.

Furthermore, there were many other devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharva kings, asura kings, garuḍa kings, kiṃnara kings, mahoraga kings, rākṣasa-yakṣas, kumbhāṇḍas, pūtanas, and kaṭapūtanas; such various hundreds of thousands of powerful spirits and deities also came and took their seats.

At that time, the World-Honored One, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, knowing that the great assembly had all gathered, was about to briefly explain for them the sequence of the profound and weighty merits of this sutra. Desiring to subdue all humans and devas, he again let out a lion’s roar and cough, and then spoke of what had never been heard before to the assembled congregation:
"This Dharma of the sutra is that which has been practiced by the Buddhas of the three periods—past, future, and present—and is able to extinguish all great sufferings and afflictions."
Therefore, the Buddhas revere this Dharma; they have practiced it, will practice it, and are practicing it now.
For this reason, O Great Being!
Those who wish to seek my body should revere the true Dharma; those who honor and serve the Dharma should do so as they would the Buddha.
Why is this? Because the Dharma is not different from the Buddha.
This person seeking the Dharma should arrive at this point.
Whether they be devas, nāgas, humans, or non-humans, those who are able to seek the Dharma will swiftly abandon all suffering.
The Buddha has taught that practicing the Dharma to eliminate suffering is the most supreme.

Therefore, when a bodhisattva seeks the Dharma of enlightenment for the sake of benefiting all the world, that bodhisattva has already bestowed the bliss of enlightenment upon all sentient beings and will swiftly attain deliverance from the great ocean of birth and death.

"When I briefly expound this subtle King of Sūtras of Samādhi to instruct the world, all mountains, rivers, and the great earth shall simultaneously quake in six ways, and at that time, all sentient beings shall cry out, 'Excellent!'"

Why is this so? When the Buddha spoke this Mahāyāna Vaipulya sūtra, the subtle and wondrous King of Great Samādhis of Mindfulness of the Buddhas—a vast ocean of great wisdom and boundless merit—countless worlds and buddha-fields numbering in the hundreds of thousands of millions of nayutas all shook in six ways with eighteen modes of movement, and emitted pure light of great brilliance that shone everywhere.
At that time, immeasurable devas from the void struck great celestial drums, their sound like the roar of thunder, while also playing harmonious, elegant, and melodious music.

Furthermore, eighty trillion nayutas of earth spirits and celestial maidens emerged from the ground holding various jeweled thrones; they approached the World-Honored One with sincere reverence and offered them as gifts.
Furthermore, there was the Gandharva King Nandika, who produced hundreds of thousands of millions of nayutas of various wondrous sounds that were most delightful.

There were also various nāgas and nāga princes who raised great dense clouds that covered the entire world, raining down celestial māndārava flowers and other exquisite blossoms that spread across the earth to a height of one hundred yojanas.

At that time, the great nāga kings of Sāgara manifested palaces in the sky, adorned with various jewels, exquisite and extraordinary; they scattered celestial sandalwood powder throughout this trichiliocosm, the world-system of the Buddha.
Furthermore, the Brahmā kings of the various heavens in the realm of form fashioned jeweled flower canopies above the Tathāgata, which completely covered the trichiliocosm.
From every part of these canopies hung various jeweled bells, all of which produced subtle and wondrous sounds, like the music of the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven.

At that time, all sentient beings in this assembly cultivated the minds of loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity; having heard the sound of the Dharma, they were overcome with joy and each, with utmost sincerity, returned once more to take refuge in the Triple Gem.
At that time, boundless sentient beings who heard the Dharma all resolved their minds upon unexcelled bodhi;
furthermore, immeasurable sentient beings all deeply resolved their minds upon the state of a pratyekabuddha;
and moreover, countless sentient beings all resolved their minds upon the bodhi of a śrāvaka.

Furthermore, there were immeasurable Kṣatriya kings, śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, vaiśyas, śūdras, elders, and householders who all attained the fruit of srotāpanna, the fruit of sakṛdāgāmin, and the fruit of anāgāmin;
additionally, there were boundless sentient beings who all realized the fruit of the unattached arhat.
At that time, when the World-Honored One had finished preaching this sutra, the entire great assembly was filled with immense joy.

The great Bodhisattvas, such as Amoghadarśin, the assembly of great Śrāvakas, and all the worldly beings—the eight classes of devas and humans, asuras, and others—having heard what the Buddha taught, were all greatly delighted and reverently accepted and practiced it.
